chapters.summary: Staff welcomes attendees to the joint Fire and Emergency Management and Housing and Buildings hearing, asks phones to be silenced, warns not to approach the dais, and tells the Chair they are ready to begin.
chapters.title: Committee staff opens joint hearing and gives procedural instructions

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning and welcome to the Committee on Fire and Emergency Management, jointly with Housing and Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please place your phone on vibrate or silent mode.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At any time during this hearing, do not approach the dais.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, we are ready to begin.

chapters.summary: Ariola opens the hearing, identifies herself as Chair, thanks Speaker Julie Menin, notes the joint hearing with Housing and Buildings and Chair Sanchez, and acknowledges committee members.
chapters.title: Chair Ariola convenes hearing and acknowledges Speaker Menin and joint committee

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Joanne Areola, Chair to the Committee on Fire and Emergency Management.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I would first like to acknowledge our speaker, Julie Menon, who is here today and who I would like to thank for her leadership on this very pressing issue that we are here to discuss.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: This hearing is being held jointly with the Committee on Housing and Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I would also like to thank Chair Pierina Sanchez for holding today's hearing and acknowledge the Fire and Emergency Management Committee members, Wong, Zhuang, Salam,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Gennaro on Zoom, Shulman on Zoom, Virginia Maloney on Zoom, De La Rosa.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I think that's that.

chapters.summary: Ariola states the hearing will cover oversight on residential fires and lithium-ion batteries plus related legislation. She cites FDNY data: over 25,000 structural fires in FY2026, more than 21,000 residential, and 292 lithium-ion battery fires in 2025, nearly 10 times 2020.
chapters.title: Ariola frames oversight on residential fires and lithium-ion battery dangers

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Today, the committee will be discussing oversight on residential fires and the dangers of lithium-ion batteries, as well as hearing related legislation.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Over the past few years, as e-bikes, e-scooters, and powered mobility devices have become more prevalent,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: the city has experienced a rapid increase in lithium-ion battery-related fires, both in residential and commercial properties.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: That not only destroys property, but results in injuries and fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: In fiscal year 2026, the FDNY experienced over 25,000 structural fires, of which more than 21,000 occurred in residential occupancies, an increase of nearly 1,300 when compared to the prior fiscal year.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: During 2025, the FDNY investigated 292 lithium-ion battery-related fires in the city, a total that is nearly 10 times the amount of reported battery-related fires in 2020.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Additionally, there has been a massive spike in fires related to lithium-ion batteries this year, including two fatal residential fires,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: one in the South Bronx and one in Sunset Park, which are still under investigation, and those resulted in the death of 10 individuals, and among them were children.

chapters.summary: Ariola notes 2023 battery safety legislation, says injuries and deaths declined until this year but incidents rose, and insists the administration must enforce city laws.
chapters.title: Ariola cites 2023 legislation and calls for enforcement

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: In 2023, the committee passed legislation related to lithium-ion battery safety,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: and intended to mitigate the safety risks related to the proper use of e-bikes and lithium-ion batteries.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Since then, although the number of injuries and deaths had declined until this year, the number of related incidences have risen.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I want to be very clear to this administration, we must have enforcement of our city's laws for them to be effective.

chapters.summary: Ariola says the committees will hear seven bills to increase awareness and regulate charging and storage of lithium-ion batteries and micromobility devices.
chapters.title: Ariola previews seven-bill package on battery charging and storage

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: To that end, the committees will also hear a package of legislation that aims to protect New Yorkers from these dangerous batteries by increasing public awareness and establishing regulations

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: regarding the charging and storage of lithium-ion batteries to help mitigate the fire safety risks proposed by these batteries and motorized bikes and scooters.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We will be hearing seven bills, six of which are in fire and emergency management and one by our accompanying...

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: co-chair and her committee.

chapters.summary: Ariola describes Intro 920 removing the residential charging exception, Intro 1174 creating an FDNY fire emergency dashboard, and Intro 1184 requiring a targeted outreach, inspection, and enforcement plan.
chapters.title: Ariola summarizes Intros 920, 1174, and 1184

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Introduction 920, sponsored by Councilmember Wong, removes the exception in the New York City Fire Code that allows the storage and charging of mobility devices in a dwelling unit in a Group R2 occupancy building.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Introduction number 1174, sponsored by Chair Sanchez, requires the fire departments maintain a publicly accessible dashboard displaying data related to fire emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The dashboard would display data including the approximate date, time, location,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: and cause of each fire over the period of the prior two years.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Users of the dashboard would be able to filter and view this information on charts and maps.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Introduction 1184, which is a bill I have introduced, requires the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: and the fire department to develop and implement a targeted outreach, inspection, and enforcement plan to mitigate the risk of death, injury, and property damage resulting from fires caused by certain powered bicycles, power mobility devices,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: and storage batteries used by such devices.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The goal of such plan would be to reduce the sale, use, and possession of the products that do not meet safety standards that are established by local laws,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: and ensure that devices and storage batteries are stored and charged in a manner consistent with the relevant fire code requirements.

chapters.summary: Ariola explains Intro 1189 penalties for uncertified devices and second-use batteries, and Intro 1202 lowering the threshold to seal retailers after two violations in two years.
chapters.title: Ariola summarizes Intros 1189 and 1202

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Introduction 1189, sponsored by Councilmember Gennaro, seeks to make it unlawful to store, handle, use, or possess a powered bicycle,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: a powered mobility device, or a storage battery for such devices unless the equipment meets the relevant standards for sale established by local law.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Bill would establish civil penalties, not criminal, for those who violate the possession ban.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Additionally, the bill would

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: amend existing penalties for the sale of such products, such that an individual would be guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by up to one year of imprisonment, in addition to the civil penalty of up to $1,000

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: for each violation.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Those are for the people who are selling these products.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Finally, a person who assembles or sells a second-use storage battery would be liable for a civil penalty of up to $1,000 and would be guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a one year of imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Introduction number 1202, sponsored by Council Member Susan Zhuang, lowers the threshold needed for the Department of Consumer

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Affairs and Worker Protection and the Fire Department to seal the premises of retailers that violate local laws

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: establishing safety standards for the distribution, sale, and lease and rental of powered bicycles, powered mobility devices, or storage of batteries for such devices.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Sealing would be permitted after the retailer receives violations on at least two occasions in a two-year period, whereas currently the

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: premises can only be sealed after a retailer receives violations on at least three occasions during a three-year period.

chapters.summary: Ariola says the committee wants to examine the spike in e-bike fires, evaluate FDNY response, consider stronger measures, and thanks committee counsel Josh Kingsley, Will Hongash, and Phyllis Cincirillo.
chapters.title: Ariola states committee goals and thanks staff

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The committee wants to examine the circumstances surrounding the current spike of e-bike-related fires over the past year, evaluate the FDNY's response,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: to this continued safety risk and consider new stronger measures to mitigate fire risks arising from these devices.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We look forward to hearing from the administration on this legislation and intend to work collaboratively

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: to find appropriate solutions to decrease the ever-growing problem of residential fires related to the storage and charging of e-bikes and lithium-ion batteries.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I would like to thank Josh Kingsley, our committee counsel, Will Hongash, our senior analyst, and my chief of staff, Phyllis Cincirillo, for working so hard to put our portion of this hearing together.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And I will now turn the microphone over to Speaker Menon for her remarks.

chapters.summary: Menin thanks the chairs, says the city is in an emergency, cites unacceptable fatalities and injuries, and argues prior bills have not solved the worsening problem.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin calls emergency hearing on battery fire crisis

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm Julie Menon, Speaker of the New York City Council.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I first of all want to thank Chair Areola and Chair Sanchez for holding this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I ask for this emergency hearing because we are in an emergency.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The numbers in terms of fatalities,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Injuries are just completely unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This is a crisis of epic proportions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The council has passed a bill after bill after bill, and yet the problem is getting worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And so we want to have a...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Real discussion, a real oversight hearing about why this is happening.

chapters.summary: Menin acknowledges lives lost and long-term injuries, leads a moment of silence, then reports FY2026 had over 25,000 structural fires, 21,000 residential, 82 fatalities, and 54 life-threatening civilian injuries.
chapters.title: Menin honors victims with moment of silence and cites fire statistics

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So let me first of all say that before I begin any more

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In terms of remarks, I want to acknowledge the lives that have been lost, in addition to the individuals that are now living with long-term medical conditions as a result of the thousands of fires that have occurred in New York City this year.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In their honor, let's pause for a moment of silence.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So as the chair said, in fiscal year 2026, New York City experienced over 25,000

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: structural fires, of which more than 21,000 occurred in apartments or houses, an increase of almost 1,300 fires compared to the prior year.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: FDNY has disclosed that more than 2,200 of these were serious fires that required response crews of at least 60 FDNY personnel.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Tragically, these fires caused 82 fatalities and 54 life-threatening injuries to civilians.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Before I say anything more, I first want to thank the members of our fire department.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We know that every day they are putting their lives on the line to save others, exemplifying what it means to be New York's bravest.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we know that they know and want to do everything they can to prevent fires in the future.

chapters.summary: Menin lists electrical, candles and smoking, heating equipment, and lithium-ion battery failures as top non-incendiary causes. She says 2026 has over 400 battery fires year-to-date, up from 292 in all of 2025, with 83 injuries and 12 deaths.
chapters.title: Menin lists top fire causes and rising lithium-ion battery data

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: According to FDNY, the top non-incendiary causes of fires in New York City are as follows.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Electrical fires due to overloaded outlets or faulty wiring, candles and smoking, heating equipment such as space heaters and electrical blankets, and unfortunately more recently,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: lithium-ion battery failures.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In recent years, the City Council has experienced a sharp increase in lithium-ion battery-related fires, largely associated with e-bikes and e-scooters.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Such fires present unique challenges to firefighting operations as they spread very quickly, they are oftentimes difficult to extinguish, and they can

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: produce toxic gases.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: As of November 2026, the city has experienced over 400 lithium ion battery fires year to date, an increase from 292

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: such fires that occurred during all of 2025.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So these numbers are just skyrocketing.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Fatalities and injuries from lithium-ion battery fires have also increased this year, rising from 51 injuries and one death in 2025

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: to 83 injuries and 12 deaths so far in 2026.

chapters.summary: Menin describes the October 28 Bronx NYCHA fire that killed a child, two teenagers, and a mother after an e-bike charging in the kitchen blocked escape, and the Sunset Park fire six days later that killed six and injured nine.
chapters.title: Menin details fatal Bronx and Sunset Park fires

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Most recently, on October 28th, a fire

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: at a Bronx NYCHA development killed a child, two teenagers, and the 33-year-old mother of one of the teens.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The cause?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: An e-bike that was charging in the apartment's kitchen caught fire, and the device's location near a doorway blocked the family's escape from their apartment.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Less than a week later, in a fire at a residential building in Sunset Park, Brooklyn, a building where the presence of e-bikes and lithium-ion batteries was being investigated by fire marshals, six people were killed and nine injured.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: These incidents are more than tragic.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: They are entirely...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Preventable and they represent safety failures at the highest level.

chapters.summary: Menin notes FDNY guidance, building rules, and DCWP enforcement but says the city must do far better, cannot accept the new normal, and wants to understand why laws are not fully enforced.
chapters.title: Menin says prevention efforts are insufficient and calls for action

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We know that FDNY issues guidance related to safe use and storage of lithium ion batteries.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We know that many buildings have issued rules pertaining to the safe storage of e-bikes and scooters.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we know that the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection has worked to get illegal or unsafe batteries off the streets and out of our stores.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But we need to do far better.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: With the proliferation of electric mobility devices in New York City,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This cannot be the new normal.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We cannot allow these fires to continue happening.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We cannot accept the loss of even one more life.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We simply cannot.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And that is why.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: we call this emergency hearing.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: At today's hearing, we are eager to understand what more we can be doing, why some of the city council laws are not being fully enforced to the highest levels,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: and really what we can do to ensure that we are protecting New Yorkers and ensure that these tragedies

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Never happen again.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'll turn it back to the chair at this point.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez thanks Menin and Ariola, identifies herself as Housing and Buildings Chair, welcomes attendees, and says the hearing stems from heartbreak over recent fires.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez welcomes attendees and frames hearing on heartbreak

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker Menon.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Chair Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Areola, and thank you both, Chair and Speaker, for centering this immense problem within our city.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Pierina Sanchez, Chair of the Committee on Housing and Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: On behalf of our committees and the council, welcome, and thank you for being with us today to discuss residential fires and the dangers of lithium-ion batteries.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We are here today, as my colleagues have said, because of heartbreak.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: In October, a lithium-ion battery caught fire in a Bronx NYCHA apartment, as the speaker just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Gratitude to Councilmember Encarnacion and her work supporting that family and that community.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Eight days later, a fire in Sunset Park killed six more New Yorkers and injured nine, and also gratitude to Councilmember Zhuang for being there for those families.

chapters.summary: Sanchez mentions fires in her district and Washington Heights, says fires are a mainstay, and recalls the Twin Parks Northwest tragedy that killed 17 after a space heater malfunction and failed self-closing doors.
chapters.title: Sanchez recounts West Bronx fire tragedies and Twin Parks

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Too many to count, it feels, in my district, in the West Bronx, includes Councilmember Feliz, and also our sister community in Washington Heights, Councilmember De La Rosa's district.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: It feels like five.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: are an unfortunate mainstay.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: For many of us, our council tenure began with the horrific Twin Parks Northwest tragedy, which claimed 17 lives after a space heater malfunctioned and doors failed to self-close in Councilmember Felice's district.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We promised then to do better.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We passed many, many bills, and the problem remains.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Gratitude always first to the first responders at FDNY, and I want to also include a special mention of New York City Emergency Management for your increased efforts to spread awareness in the West Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What makes these tragedies the most difficult to bear is that we know so many of the risks.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Year after year, we see fires caused by the same dangers.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Faulty electrical wiring, as the speaker has mentioned, especially concerning in our aging housing stock.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Smoking materials, unsafe batteries in an increasing manner, and candles left unattended.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: As Twin Parks so painfully reminded us, space heaters also are deadly within our homes.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But these are not new dangers.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We know what they are.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The question is whether we're doing everything in our power to prevent them and why it is that New York families continue to pay the price with their lives.

chapters.summary: Sanchez says 82 New Yorkers have died in fires in 2026, nearly double last year at this time, and says the Council wants to understand agency prevention efforts and what more can be done.
chapters.title: Sanchez cites 82 fire deaths and asks what more agencies can do

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: 82 New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: 82 New Yorkers have perished already in fires in 2026, which is nearly

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: double the number of fire deaths at this time last year.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We look forward to understanding better what our agencies are doing to prevent these tragedies and what more can be done.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The Council has strengthened self-closing door protections, restricted unsafe rebuilt batteries, and established a battery trade-in program.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But we must also protect the delivery workers who rely on these devices to earn a living.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: They did not manufacture dangerous batteries.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Manufacturers, distributors, retailers, and delivery companies must be a part, an important part, the center of ensuring safe equipment is accessible and hopefully also affordable.

chapters.summary: Sanchez says when prevention fails families lose homes and face an unaffordable housing market. She notes Councilmember Gutierrez's Back Home Unit legislation and asks for a progress report eight months in.
chapters.title: Sanchez addresses displacement and Back Home Unit progress

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Finally, what happens when prevention fails?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: New Yorkers are lost.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: They perish.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Families lose their homes.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Land and temporary hotels face a housing market that so many cannot afford.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Councilmember Gutierrez's legislation from

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: several years ago, required the administration to coordinate assistance for displaced families through the creation of the back home unit.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Eight months into its creation, we're asking for a progress report today.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We've seen the QR codes on the fire trucks, but what is that unit actually in, how is that, excuse me, how is that unit actually integrated into emergency responses?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I will leave off the summary of the bills as Councilmember Areola has already addressed them.

chapters.summary: Sanchez says she opposed similar legislation previously and remains strongly opposed to penalties for possessing noncompliant devices and criminal penalties on certain sales, standing with Deliveristas Unidos. She thanks her team and Housing and Buildings staff.
chapters.title: Sanchez opposes Intro 1189 and thanks staff

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But I do want to address Intro 1189 in particular as it is a piece of legislation that was heard in a different form in the previous council.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I personally objected to this legislation during the previous administration and the previous council and remain strongly opposed because it would impose penalties for possessing noncompliant devices.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And criminal penalties on certain sales, shifting some of that burden onto the low-income workers and vulnerable New Yorkers who may unknowingly purchase unsafe products.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I stand with Deliveri Estados Unidos in opposing that legislation.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So I look forward to a discussion today focused on prevention, accountability, and a city that helps families get back home.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'd like to take this opportunity to thank my team, Deputy Chiefs Ben Ratner and Kim Castellanos, Gerard Fernandez, Marcus Kahn, Malia Sardinia, the district team, Maria Jose, Soraya, Oriana, and our interns, Emily, Jeralyn, and Marcus.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'd also like to thank the Housing and Buildings Committee team, including Senior Legislative Counsel Austin Malone,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Legislative Council Billy Eck, Senior Policy Analyst Jose Conde and Dirk Spencer, and Finance Analyst Carla Naranjo.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And I just wanted to take a moment, I know this hearing today is focused on fires, fire prevention, fire response, but to also acknowledge the pain in Flatbush and Councilmember Lewis's community

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: and ensure that we're talking about prevention of as many tragedies as we can.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks the Speaker, recognizes Gennaro, notes Commissioner Bonsignore has joined, and asks Zhuang to speak. Zhuang says her district lost six lives on November 5, including an immigrant family from China, and explains Intro 1202 would allow closure after two violations instead of three.
chapters.title: Ariola recognizes Gennaro and calls Zhuang; Zhuang describes Sunset Park fire and Intro 1202

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We'd like to recognize Councilmember Gennaro to speak about his bill.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, so we are joined today by Commissioner Lillian.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Before we get to that, Councilmember Zhuang, would you like to speak about your bill?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Speaker, to hold this emergency hearing.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: On November 5, my district lost six lives.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: They are immigrants.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: There's one family, I know them personally, just moved here two months ago from China.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So it's devastating in the community to see the fire.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And this is not the first time we had a fire in the community.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: About a few months ago, we had another fire caused by e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: But this tragedy happened in November 5, it's still under investigation, we don't know what's the reason, but unsafe e-bikes and their

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: lithium-ion batteries have caused many devastating fires across the city and take many lives.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We must regulate this before more lives are lost.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And that includes holding those selling them accountable.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Intro 1202 make it easier for New York City to shut down retail establishments that are selling unsafe batteries and e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: It could permit the Department of Consumer and Work Protection to close such a...

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: store after two such violations rather than three.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: It could be argued on the first violation the store owner does not aware that selling those items is illegal, but after the first violation they are aware and must be held accountable.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Lives are on the line and we cannot wait

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: for yet another tragedy.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I call on my colleagues to join me and support this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks Zhuang, notes Councilmember Carl Wilson has joined, and calls De La Rosa. De La Rosa describes the May 4 fire at 207 Dyckman Street that killed four neighbors, destroyed eight apartments, and displaced about 100 people, noting 117 open violations and broken self-closing doors.
chapters.title: Ariola acknowledges Carl Wilson and calls De La Rosa; De La Rosa recounts deadly Dyckman Street fire

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We've also been joined by Councilmember Carl Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask Councilmember De La Rosa to have her statement.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Carmen De La Rosa, and I'm proud to co-prime sponsor Intros 174 and 1175 along Chair Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker Menon, Chair Riola, and of course, Chair Sanchez for convening this joint hearing.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I'd also like to thank the Commissioner, our first responders, and our agency partners.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: On May 4th, a fire tore through 207 Dyckman Street in my district.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Four of our neighbors lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Yolani Diaz and her mother, Ana Mirta Lantigua, Lance Garcia, and his mother, Annie De La Cruz.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Eight apartments were destroyed, and about 100 people were displaced.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The fire began with a discarded cigarette, but what made it deadly was a building the city already knew was in distress.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: 207 Dyckman Street had 117 open violations and had been placed in HP.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Alternative Enforcement Program in January.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Inspectors cited broken self-closing doors three days before the fire broke.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And HPD had sued the same owner a week earlier over hazards next door at 209 Dyckman.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Fire officials said open doors left flames race up the building's only staircase.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Think about what the public paid for that night and after.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Nearly 200 firefighters and EMS personnel responded.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The Red Cross sheltered families on MTA buses while HPD worked to find them temporary housing.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And the city issued a full vacate order on the building.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: When we wait for a building in distress to burn, we pay for it in lives, in displacement, and in public resources.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa says the city had over 21,000 residential fires and 82 deaths in FY2026, and that electrical wiring and lithium-ion batteries are major causes. She explains Intro 1175 would study electrical capacity and Intro 1174 would create a public fire dashboard.
chapters.title: De La Rosa links fire prevention to displacement and explains Intros 1174 and 1175

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We cannot keep responding after the fact.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Fires in our homes are rising, and in fiscal year 2026, the city had more than 21,000 residential fires, nearly 1,300 more than the year before, and 82 New Yorkers died.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Since 2021, faulty electrical wiring has caused about one in six fires investigated by the FDNY, second only to arson and lithium-ion batteries have caused another 6.7%.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: This year alone, we have seen 400 lithium-ion battery fires and 12 deaths compared with 292 fires and one death in all of 2025.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Our older buildings were never wired.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: for e-bikes, space heaters, the way that families live today.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Intro 1175s lets us be proactive.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: If we study the electrical capacity of our older buildings, we can identify a building in distress before it catches fire, prioritize upgrades, and keep tenants in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Preventing fires is also how we fight displacement.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And Intro 1174 brings transparency to an already difficult process.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Right now, residents, community boards, and even elected officials struggled to get basic information about fires on our own blocks, in our own streets, in our districts.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: A public dashboard showing when fires happen, when and why will help us to see patterns and send resources where they are needed most.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Families in Upper Manhattan and all across our city deserve more than a response.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: They deserve prevention.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I look forward to the hearing from the administration, the advocates, and the public today, and I thank you all for your service.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks De La Rosa and calls Feliz. Feliz thanks the chairs and FDNY, says over 400 e-bike fires this year is a textbook fire safety crisis, notes prior measures like UL certification and trade-in program, and argues the city must consider stricter measures.
chapters.title: Ariola calls Feliz; Feliz calls situation a fire safety crisis and says more is needed

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Council Member Feliz, you want to make a statement?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs Areola and Sanchez and Speaker Menon for this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Also, thank you to the fire department for all the work that you do on the issue of fire safety.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What we're seeing today is the textbook definition of a fire safety crisis.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: This year, we've had over 400 fires due to defective e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: This is more fires than we've ever had due to lithium-ion batteries.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: These fires, as we know, are incredibly dangerous.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: They happen with very little to no notice.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: These batteries could even explode just by turning on the e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: These are fires that also escalate extremely quickly and also fires that are difficult to extinguish.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: These fires are dangerous.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: They destroy our homes, and they also put all of our lives at risk.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We've taken many measures on this issue, including my legislation that prohibited the sale of uncertified e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We also created a trade-in program.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We also passed legislation requiring that the delivery apps also play a role.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: In resolution of this issue, but based on the fact that this issue has only worsened over the years, that makes one point extremely clear.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What we've done is nowhere near enough.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: The issue, again, has only worsened.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: forward to today's conversation and look forward to discussing the many measures before this committee today.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: As we all know, this is not an easy issue, but given that this issue has only worsened, I think it's time for us to think about stricter measures so that we can finally put an end to this fire safety crisis.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We cannot go on with this issue for another million years.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks Feliz, tries Gennaro on Zoom, then asks Wong to speak. Wong says residents should not worry about e-bike batteries charging in neighboring apartments, cites a recent Bronx fire that killed four family members including an 11-year-old, and explains Intro 920 would remove the personal-use exemption for storing and charging up to five mobility devices. He asks what FDNY can enforce and what authority it needs.
chapters.title: Ariola calls Wong; Wong introduces Intro 920 and raises enforcement concerns

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Councilmember Gennaro, can you hear us now?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Council Member Wong, would you like to make your statement while we're waiting?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Areola and Chair Sanchez, for holding this important hearing.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: and for hearing my bill in show 920.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I also want to thank Speaker Menon for bringing attention to this issue and our firefighters and first responders who put their lives on the line every day.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: New Yorkers should not have to worry about an e-bike battery charging in a neighboring apartment or the apartment above it.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: That could put their entire building at risk.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And yet that's exactly the danger we're continuing to face every day.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We had hundreds of lithium-ion battery fires in New York City this year with lives lost and many more people injured.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Just last month, four members of one family, including an 11-year-old,

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: The 12-year-old boy died in a Bronx apartment, fire involving an e-bike battery.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: These tragedies should never become something we simply accept.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: That's why I introduced Intro 920.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Right now, our fire code allows up to five battery-powered mobility devices to be stored and charged inside certain residential apartments under a personal use exemption.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My bill would remove that exception and require compliance with applicable fire safety standards.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: By passing legislation is only half the battle.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We also need meaningful enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My office regularly receives complaints about batteries being charged inside homes and on private property.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We bring those concerns to the FDNY, but too often...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We're left wondering what happened next or if any at all.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I understand there are legal limitations when it comes to entering private properties, but we need answers.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What can the FDNY actually enforce?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What evidence is needed and what additional authority does the department need?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We cannot keep asking residents to report dangerous conditions without giving them confidence that those reports lead somewhere.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks Wong and calls on Gennaro, who has difficulty unmuting. Gennaro apologizes, thanks Ariola and Sanchez, praises Speaker Menin's leadership, says his bill has been discussed, and yields.
chapters.title: Ariola recognizes Gennaro; Gennaro thanks chairs and associates with Speaker Menin

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Councilmember Gennaro.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You can unmute on your end.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Welcome.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I had difficulty unmuting, and so obviously I'm on now.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Chair Areola, for having this hearing and your leadership.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I think you did a great job about talking about Intro 1189.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I appreciate Council Member Chair Sanchez for your leadership as well.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Also, the Speaker's leadership is, you know, foremost.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I really have nothing to add to all of the remarks.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I think my bill has been, you know, put out there and talked about, and I wish to associate myself with the comments of Speaker Minnit.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: With that, I yield and look forward to a great hearing.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks Gennaro, introduces FDNY Commissioner Bonsignore, First Deputy Commissioner Flynn, Chief Correo, Chief Esposito, HPD's Josh Cuccero, and DOB's Yegel Shamaya. She notes DCWP was invited but absent and questions were submitted. Staff administers the oath.
chapters.title: Ariola introduces agency panel and administers oath

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Now we will move on to introducing the dais.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We are joined by New York City Fire Department Commissioner Lillian Bonsignor, First Deputy Commissioner Daniel Flynn, Chief Thomas Correo,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Chief John Esposito.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: HPD, we have Josh Cuccero.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And from the Department of Buildings, we have Yegel Shamaya.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I just want to make note that we did invite the Department of Consumer Affairs and Worker Protection.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We have many hearings that are going on today that they were needed at.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: However, we did submit questions.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: To them and the fire department was nice enough to have those questions and by proxy answer, but we as

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: both chairs and the speaker will be meeting with the Department of

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: consumer affairs and worker protection separately to have a conversation.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Today is a very busy day at City Hall.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Commissioner, for being here, for bringing a team that you've assembled that can answer questions.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And please, Josh, our committee council will now administer the oath.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.text: Can you just raise your right hand and affirm that?

chapters.summary: Bonsignore greets officials, introduces her team, and says 2026 has 90 fire fatalities so far, compared with 63 in 2025, 77 in 2024, 104 in 2023, and 97 in 2022. She attributes the increase partly to a cold start to the year and more space heater use.
chapters.title: Commissioner Bonsignore begins FDNY testimony on fire fatalities

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Commissioner, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Good morning, Speaker Manon, Chair Areola, and the members of the Fire and Emergency Management Committee, and Chair Sanchez and the members of the Housing and Buildings Committee.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: My name is Lillian Bonsignor, and I am the Commissioner of the New York City Fire Department.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I am joined today by Daniel Flynn, our first deputy commissioner, John Esposito, chief of department, and Tom Correo, the chief of fire prevention.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I am also joined by Associate Commissioner Josh Cuchero and Deputy Commissioner Patrick Love from the Department of Housing, Preservation, and Development.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And the first deputy commissioner, Yigal Shamash, from the Department of Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to discuss residential fires and the dangers of lithium ion batteries.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: This has been a busy year for the FDMY fire operations.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Unfortunately,

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We have had a large number of fire fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I'll discuss some of the trends that we've seen, how we are proactively addressing those trends, and some ways for the city as a whole to make improvements.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: As of today, we have 90 fire fatalities in 2026.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Recent years have included fatality totals of 63 in 2025, 77 in 2024,

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: There are several reasons that fire deaths are up this year.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We had an extremely cold beginning of the year with prolonged code blue conditions.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We know from experience that cold weather means more people are staying home.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: There's increased use of space heaters and other heating equipment and a higher occurrences of fire.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We experienced 11 fire fatalities in January alone.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: That set us on a trend of higher numbers right from the start.

chapters.summary: Bonsignore says many fatal fires fall into categories: 19 incendiary, 18 electrical, 9 lithium-ion battery, 7 smoking, 5 candles, and 3 cooking. She also describes a Bronx gas explosion after a stove was removed.
chapters.title: Bonsignore breaks down causes of fatal fires

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Additionally, many of this year's fatal fires have included multiple fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: The Bureau of Fire Investigation analyzes each major fire and determines the cause and origin.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Many of the fatal fires this year have fallen into a small group of categories.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: 19 fatalities were related to fires that were incendiary.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: An incendiary fire is one in which a person intentionally ignites a fire in an area or under circumstances where there should not be a fire.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: category includes suicides, self-immolation, and the intentional ignition of items such as flammable liquids or cardboard boxes.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: In addition to these 19 fatalities, there was also a fire fatality at a residence in the Bronx

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: that occurred after an individual deliberately removed a stove from the wall, leading to a gas explosion that killed one person and injured 15 others.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: 18 fatalities occurred during fires that were related to electrical issues, including electrical wiring and power strips.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Nine fatalities were related to lithium ion batteries this year.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Seven were related to fires caused by smoking.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Five were related to candles.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And three were related to cooking.

chapters.summary: Bonsignore says older buildings with pipe chases, dumbwaiter shafts, voids, and cocklofts spread fire rapidly. Heavy clutter, noncompliant self-closing doors, and illegally subdivided residences also impede firefighters, as seen in the Sunset Park fire.
chapters.title: Bonsignore cites building conditions that spread fatal fires

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Another factor that has played a role in many fatal fires has been the age of the buildings involved in the fatal fires.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Older buildings have features such as pipe chases, dumbwaiter shafts, voids, and cocklofts, and these spaces contribute to the rapid spread of the fire.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Residences with heavy clutter conditions also make it difficult for firefighters to suppress the fire and

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: more challenging to locate potential victims.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: The Housing Maintenance Code requires many types of doors in residential buildings to be self-closing.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: But we have continued to see issues with doors that do not comply and residents leaving doors open when fleeing a fire.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Doors remaining open during a fire enable smoke to spread throughout the building, imperiling neighbors who may be located even several floors away.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We have experienced issues with illegally subdivided residences.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: At the fire in Sunset Park that resulted in six deaths, FDNY members arrived only three minutes after receiving a 911 call.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: However, they found that in the first and second floor apartments had been subdivided into multiple single room occupancies.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: This remains of several, the remains of several bedrooms contained small, small portable refrigerators powered by lightweight extension cords, as well as key locks on bedroom doors.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: One bedroom even had been subdivided by sealing up an existing doorway opening, further altering the original apartment configuration and making it significantly more challenging for first responders to reach trapped residents.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Each of these challenges points

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: to the need for continued education and outreach to building owners and residents.

chapters.summary: Bonsignore says lithium-ion battery deaths fell from 18 in 2023 to 6 in 2024 and 1 in 2025, but fires rose from 268 to 279 to 292, then jumped to 421 as of November 13, 2026, with 9 fatalities.
chapters.title: Bonsignore reports lithium-ion battery fire and fatality trends

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: This Sunset Park fire has not been determined.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: It is still under investigation.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Lithium ion batteries.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Following 18 deaths in fires caused by lithium ion batteries in 2023, that number decreased to six deaths in 2024 and only a single death in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: However, over that time, the number of lithium-ion battery fires grew each year,

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: This year, the number of fires have jumped to 421 as of November 13th.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: With this increase in fires, we have seen the number of fatalities in these fires also increase to nine.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: This is a concerning increase, and we have intensified our efforts to educate and enforce around this issue.

chapters.summary: Bonsignore says the Lithium-Ion Battery Task Force visits every bike shop, responds to complaints, performed 843 inspections last year and nearly 500 this year, and has cracked down on uncertified sales. She notes older uncertified devices remain in use and supports trade-in programs.
chapters.title: Bonsignore describes FDNY lithium-ion task force and inspections

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: The FDNY's Lithium-Ion Battery Task Force visits every bike shop in the city and responds to complaints and tips about potentially unsafe batteries.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: This group performed a total of 843 lithium-ion battery-related inspections last year and had performed nearly 500 such inspections this year.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So far.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We have cracked down on the sale of uncertified batteries and bikes to the point that we now only rarely come across individuals in those shops selling uncertified products.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We urge everyone to alert the fire department if they become aware of unscrupulous sellers engaging in transactions for uncertified products.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We receive complaints.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: When we receive complaints, FDNY inspectors and fire marshals respond within hours.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: However, we also know that there are thousands of bikes and batteries being used that were sold prior to the strict regulations going into effect.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: As these products age, it is likely that they are contributing to the increase in fires.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We would like to encourage more programs designed to replace older devices with new ones, particularly where the older ones are not certified.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And we are committed to working with our fellow city agencies to explore expanding trade-in programs.

chapters.summary: Bonsignore describes social media, paid media, partnerships, PSAs with council members, a five-week FDNY Foundation campaign targeting ethnic media, and updates to the apartment building emergency response guide. She also notes fire code revision is considering lithium-ion battery changes.
chapters.title: Bonsignore outlines public outreach and education campaigns

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: The fire department is also continuing an aggressive public outreach and messaging campaign about the importance of using certified devices in a safe manner.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We have produced social media and paid media campaigns to provide guidance.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We have also collaborated with numerous partners inside and outside of government, including the mayor's office,

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: our fellow city agencies and elected officials.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We have even enlisted members of the city council to appear in PSAs.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And I invite any of the members here today to work with us on a video to share educational messaging to your constituents via social media.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: In addition to the existing educational methods that we carry out through instructional programs, social media, and news media, we will soon be using a grant from the FDNY Foundation to fund a five-week educational

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: paid media campaign on this topic.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: The campaign will target users and potential users of these devices in a wide variety of outlets, including ethnic media

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: and publications that communicate in a wide variety of languages, so that we can reach New Yorkers who may not regularly access English language media.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We will be devoting a substantial portions of the 2027 apartment building emergency response guide,

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: emergency preparedness guide, which is distributed to apartment building residents and staff to the fire concerns involving electrical issues and lithium ion batteries.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Additionally, the technical committee for the New York City fire code revision process is currently considering proposed code changes on the topic of lithium ion batteries.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: This technology is not going away, but the fire department will continue

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: innovating and working with partners, including City Council, to make its use as safe as possible.

chapters.summary: Bonsignore says FDNY shares the transparency goal but maintaining a dashboard for all fires would be time-consuming and resource-intensive, and cause is not always determined for smaller fires. She wants to discuss defining covered incidents usefully and manageably.
chapters.title: Bonsignore comments on Intro 1174 fire dashboard

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: legislation.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Introduction 1174.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: This bill introduced by Councilmember Purina Sanchez would require the fire department to maintain a public dashboard displaying information

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: such as the location, date, time, and cause of every fire that occurred during the calendar year and previous year.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We share the goal of transparency and providing information to the public.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Under this proposal, though, maintaining such a dashboard for all fires would be time-consuming and resource-intensive.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Some aspects of the required information may not be available.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: In particular, the Bureau of Fire Investigation does not always determine a cause for smaller fires.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We would be interested in discussing potential ways to define the covered incidents in a way that would be useful to the public and manageable to maintain.

chapters.summary: Bonsignore says DOB has technical expertise, owners must maintain safe buildings, and compliance with the 2025 Electrical Code may be triggered by repairs, upgrades, or added loads. She notes challenges like access to private residential buildings but supports collaboration.
chapters.title: Bonsignore comments on Intro 1175 electrical capacity study

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Introduction 1175.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: This bill introduced by Councilmember Purina Sanchez would require the Department of Buildings in collaboration with the Department of Housing Preservation and Development

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: and the fire department to conduct periodic electrical capacity studies and determine which buildings need an electrical panel

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: upgrade to accommodate a higher electrical capacity.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: The Department of Buildings has technical expertise in this area.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: They note that owners are required to maintain buildings in a safe condition and in compliance with all applicable code and rule provisions.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: With regard to existing buildings, compliance with the 2025 New York City Electrical Code may be triggered when any repairs or upgrades are made or when new electrical loads are added

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: that exceed the capacity of the existing system.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Under the existing building code, which goes into effect on July 17, 2027, upgrades to a building's electrical system may also be required when substantial alterations are made.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: It is ultimately the owner's responsibility to hire licensed professionals to evaluate their systems and perform any necessary repairs.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Or upgrades to their building's electrical system.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: DOB shares the council's concerns for electrical safety and commitment to modernizing the city's aging housing stock, but implementing the requirements of 1175

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: presents a number of challenges, such as obtaining access to private residential buildings,

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: including individual tenant spaces.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: DOB recognizes the importance of this critical issue and its impact on New Yorkers, ensuring that the city

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: aging residential buildings have safe and reliable electrical infrastructure is essential to protecting tenants and first responders.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: But both FDNY and DOB look forward to collaborating with the council and agency partners on this issue.

chapters.summary: Bonsignore supports the goal but says no product currently has UL certification for fireproof or fire-resistant battery charging containers, and FDNY testing has not found any that withstand lithium-ion battery fires.
chapters.title: Bonsignore comments on Intro 582 fireproof battery containers

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Introduction 582.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: This bill introduced by Councilmember Gutierrez would require all businesses that use bicycles for commercial purposes to provide motor-assisted

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: operators with fireproof or fire-resistant containers suitable for charging removable storage batteries.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Used to power the bicycles.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: While we appreciate and support the goal of this legislation, it's important to stress that no product currently has a UL certification for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Anecdotally, the fire department has tested many of these products on our own, and we have not found

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: any that stand up to the lithium ion battery fire.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Once such a product does exist, we would be in favor of the requirement of this legislation.

chapters.summary: Bonsignore says removing the Group R2 dwelling unit exemption would significantly impact New Yorkers who rely on micromobility devices, and FDNY is working to balance safety with those needs.
chapters.title: Bonsignore comments on Intro 920 residential charging exception

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Introduction 920.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: This bill introduced by Councilmember Wong would remove the exemption in Section 309.3 of the New York City Fire Code that allows the storage and charging of mobility devices in a dwelling unit in a Group 2

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: a group R2 occupancy bill.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We know that this legislation would have a significant impact upon the ever-growing number of New Yorkers who rely on micromobility devices for transportation and in some cases their livelihood.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: The department is working with the administration and the council to achieve the right balance to optimize safety for everyone.

chapters.summary: Bonsignore says FDNY already performs targeted inspections and education, and DCWP has worked with FDNY under Local Law 49 to inspect and educate businesses. Both agencies look forward to working with the Council.
chapters.title: Bonsignore comments on Intro 1184 outreach and enforcement plan

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Introduction 1184.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: This bill introduced by Chair Areola would require the Department

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: of Consumer and Worker Protection and the Fire Department to develop and implement a targeted outreach, inspection, and enforcement plan to mitigate the risk of death, injury, and property damage

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: caused by powered mobility devices by reducing the sale, use, and possession

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: of the products that do not meet safety standards established by local law and ensuring that the devices and batteries are stored and charged in a manner consistent with the fire code requirements.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Fire inspectors perform numerous targeted inspections

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: and respond frequently and swiftly to any reports that they receive of illicit sale or use of improper batteries or mobility devices.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: The FDNY's Fire Safety Education Unit and the Office of Public Information currently

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: perform a great deal of educational outreach on this topic.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: DCWP has worked closely with the FDNY to develop similar educational materials under Local Law 49

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: in 2024 and continues to work closely with the FDNY to inspect and educate businesses on the dangers of lithium-ion batteries.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: DCWP currently prioritizes inspections of businesses with previous violations, working to bring them into compliance.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Both agencies look forward to working with the Council on this legislation.

chapters.summary: Bonsignore supports increasing penalties for retailers but says criminalizing individual possession would affect many New Yorkers and is difficult to enforce because certification is hard to determine after years of use. DCWP opposes the bill due to impacts on delivery workers.
chapters.title: Bonsignore comments on Intro 1189 penalties for uncertified devices

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Introduction 1189.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: This bill introduced by Council Member Gennaro would amend the administrative code to increase penalties for violations involving the sale, lease, or rental of uncertified powered mobility devices and batteries.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: It would also amend the fire code to prohibit storing, handling, using, or possessing uncertified bikes and batteries.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: The fire department is anxious to see uncertified devices removed from circulation, and we support increasing the penalties for retailers who sell or lease dangerous devices.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: However, criminalizing the individual possession of uncertified devices would have a significant impact on a large number of New Yorkers, and we think this step should be part of a conversation

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: with other administration partners and the council about how to balance such a change with opportunities for trade-in programs or other methods to enable

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: e-bike users to rid themselves of uncertified devices.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Additionally, from a practical standpoint, enforcement of a ban on possession of uncertified batteries would be very challenging, given how difficult it could be to determine whether batteries and devices

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: that have been in use for years are in fact uncertified.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We have

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: consulted with the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection on this bill.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: DCWP also shares the Council's goal to rid the streets of unsafe micromobility devices.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: However, DCWP opposes this bill due to significant concerns of unintended consequences

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: that would most heavily impact delivery workers, many of whom are immigrants with limited English proficiency.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: They note that the delivery workers could face losing their livelihoods and having their lives upended through the confiscation of the device they use every day to make a living.

chapters.summary: Bonsignore says FDNY and DCWP support lowering the threshold for sealing retailers that violate safety standards for powered mobility devices.
chapters.title: Bonsignore comments on Intro 1202 sealing premises

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Introduction 1202.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: This bill introduced by Councilmember Schwang would lower the threshold needed for DCWP or the fire department to seal the premises of retailers that violate local laws establishing safety standards for the distribution,

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: sale, lease, and rental of powered mobility devices.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: The fire department and the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection would support this change.

chapters.summary: Bonsignore describes rescues at fatal fires in Coney Island, East 187th Street, Dyckman Street, East 209th Street, and Sunset Park, including a probationary firefighter removing an unconscious person and firefighters freeing people trapped behind window bars.
chapters.title: Bonsignore highlights heroic FDNY rescues at fatal fires

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
