utterances.text: I want to conclude by taking a moment to highlight the work of FDNY members at several fatal fires that saved the lives of others.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: At a fatal fire in Coney Island in August,

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: a probationary firefighter who was just weeks out of the academy, successfully located and removed an unconscious individual from an apartment with a head

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: clutter condition, delivering him to EMS rescue medics who immediately performed life-saving medical care.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: A fatal fire on East 187th Street in June could have been much worse but for the several heroic rescues that Ladder 56 performed.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Including using a portable ladder to rescue a resident who was trapped at a windowsill.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Firefighters made additional rescues at fatal fires on Dyckman Street in Manhattan and on East 209th Street in the Bronx, including using a tower ladder to remove several individuals, one of them an infant,

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: from the upper floors of that building.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: In the Sunset Park fire, in the beginning of November, six people tragically lost their lives, but two others were saved when firefighters were able to free them after being trapped behind window bars.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: FDNY firefighters and fire officers continue putting themselves in harm's way in service of their fellow New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And when they make heroic rescues, they hand those patients off to the waiting arms of the highly trained and supremely capable EMTs and paramedics.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Who begin providing emergency room level medical care immediately.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: FDNY members work together to give each patient their best chance to survive.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I am immensely proud

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: and appreciative of the work that these heroes continue to do.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks Bonsignore, acknowledges Public Advocate Jumaane Williams, and yields to Menin. Menin asks how many lithium-ion battery fires involve uncertified, second-use, or aftermarket devices. Flynn says it is very difficult to determine post-fire because cells can be ejected up to 60 feet and marshals rely on owner interviews.
chapters.title: Ariola thanks Commissioner and yields to Menin; Menin asks how many battery fires involve uncertified devices

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner, for your comprehensive testimony.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I just want to acknowledge that our public advocate, Jumaane Williams, has joined us, and I will yield now to Speaker Menon to begin her questioning.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much, and thank you, Commissioner, for your comments today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We have a lot of questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So of the fires caused by lithium-ion batteries, how many involve batteries that are uncertified, second-use, or aftermarket devices?

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I'm going to turn this over to First Deputy Commissioner Dan Flynn to talk about lithium-ion batteries.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Good morning, and thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Deputy Commissioner, I don't mean to cut you off, but I just want to note that I was remiss in not noting that Majority Leader Abreu is present.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: That is something we try to determine, but it's very difficult to determine post-fire.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Just to get an idea of what these look like post-fire, the sleeve for the battery is filled with individual cells.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: When the battery fails, those cells could be ejected up to 60 feet from the point of failure.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So for our marshals, they go out there, they try to determine what type of device was used, really by interviews with the people that own the device.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So it's very hard for the marshals to do a direct investigation or examination of that battery post-fire.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So that information, unfortunately, is very difficult for us to do.

chapters.summary: Menin asks why the administration opposes Council efforts to strengthen regulation given nine battery fatalities this year versus one last year. Flynn says they are not opposed to strengthening regulation and notes federal lithium-ion battery legislation passed the Senate.
chapters.title: Menin asks why administration opposes strengthening battery regulation

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So given that there were nine lithium-ion battery fatalities related to the batteries, fatalities this year alone, versus one last year, why is the administration opposing?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: council's efforts to try to strengthen regulation around lithium ion batteries.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I don't believe that we are opposed to strengthening regulation.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And if I could also point out in a timely manner last night, yesterday, the Senate did approve a lithium ion battery bill on the federal level that we had been advocating for for several years.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We've made

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: almost a half a dozen trips down to DC to advocate for that bill, which would be very similar to Councilmember Felice's bill.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Local Law 39, which would prohibit the sale or importation of devices that do not meet that UL standard.

chapters.summary: Menin notes the administration opposes amending the fire code to prohibit possessing uncertified bikes and batteries. Flynn says they oppose the bill in current form because it would vilify people who rely on the devices and enforcement after point of sale is nearly impossible.
chapters.title: Flynn explains opposition to criminalizing possession of uncertified devices

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm just going to interrupt because the commissioner just testified that you, that the administration is against a bill to amend the fire code to prohibit its storing, handling, using, or possessing uncertified bikes and batteries.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We are against that bill in its current form, just because we do not want to vilify the people that rely so heavily on these devices.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: As Council Member Sanchez mentioned, we understand the value of these devices to members of our community, and we just want them to use them safely.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We're not saying that lithium-ion technology is a bad thing.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We understand that it poses a tremendous value to all of us.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We want people to just use high-quality products, safe products.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: The bill in its current form, I think, would make it impossible for some of our communities to exercise their livelihood and who rely on these batteries.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So is there a way to fix the bill and put the onus on the third-party apps?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We would be welcome any other bills to review those.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We really want to focus on the sale, the point of sale.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: That's where we can really determine whether these are certified batteries or not.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Once that consumer walks out of that store, it's almost impossible for us to determine whether that battery is certified or not.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: The way we determine whether the battery is certified by direct examination,

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Is from an adhesive sticker.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So once that leaves the store, there's no obligation on the consumer to keep that sticker on the battery.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And given the elements here, and most people in our city are using these for a commercial purpose, that sticker could easily fall off and it would make it impossible for us to enforce

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: any legislation that would have us examine batteries and determine whether they are certified or they're not post point of sale.

chapters.summary: Menin asks what conversations FDNY has had with the Consumer Product Safety Commission. Flynn says he testified before CPSC, the agency will be mandated to create a rule within 180 days after federal bill signing, and FDNY regularly shares evidence with CPSC investigators.
chapters.title: Menin asks about CPSC conversations on uncertified batteries

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So on the issue of these uncertified batteries, Commissioner, what conversations have you had with the Consumer Product Safety Commission to date since you've been in your position?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I've actually, I've testified in front of the Consumer Product Safety Commission related to this issue.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: The Consumer Product Safety Commission has been mandated now, well, once the

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: President signs a bill, which we are optimistic that he will, they will be mandated within 180 days to come up with a rule on how to regulate these devices.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we have a great relationship with them.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: They're investigators here in the city.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We communicate with regularly.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Anytime we have a fire that the marshals determine to be lithium ion in nature, we allow them to examine any evidence that we've collected.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: This way they can monitor on the national level to make sure they're not seeing trends in certain products.

chapters.summary: Menin asks whether fires occur while charging, in use, or in storage. Flynn says evidence shows fires occur much more often while not charging, but the danger exists either way, so people should follow safety messaging.
chapters.title: Flynn says battery fires occur more often while not charging

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Are the fires mostly occurring while devices or batteries are charging, or is it in use, or is it during storage, or all of the above?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: That's a great question, and I think we all assumed that these fires were occurring while charging when we started out investigating these.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: But our evidence has shown that they actually occur much more often while not charging.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We do know that they pose a danger whether charging or not charging.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we want people to heed our safety messaging as if the charging or not charging does not really make a difference.

chapters.summary: Menin asks how closely FDNY works with DCWP. Flynn describes the e-safety task force with inspectors and marshals working daily with DCWP, and reports 471 inspections, 255 FDNY summonses, 55 criminal summons violation orders, and 8 locations meeting the sealing threshold.
chapters.title: Menin asks about FDNY and DCWP coordination on dangerous batteries

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: How closely is FDNY working with DCWP to identify these dangerous lithium-ion batteries or to ensure that users of these batteries understand safe use, charging, and storage?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: As the Commissioner mentioned, we developed an e-safety task force.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So that task force consists of our...

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Bureau of Fire Prevention inspectors from the Special Inspections Unit.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: That consists of one chief inspector, one deputy chief inspector, one supervising inspector, eight actual inspectors.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We have two marshals that go out, and we do that in conjunction with DCWP on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: The commissioner mentioned some of our numbers earlier.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: To date this year, we've conducted 471 inspections at these commercial establishments to ensure that they are in compliance with the laws that have already been enacted.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Of those inspections, we've issued 255 FDNY summonses.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: 55 violation orders for criminal summonses.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And of those, we've identified eight locations that have met the threshold for sealing.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So that is another bill that has been proposed.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And we would be supportive of any bills that would increase the penalties.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: For selling these dangerous devices.

chapters.summary: Menin asks how inspection numbers compare to prior years. Flynn says 467 inspections in 2023, 585 in 2024, 843 in 2025, and 471 year-to-date. Menin asks why they are significantly down; Flynn says inspections have been effective and most stores have been visited more than once.
chapters.title: Menin asks why inspections dropped compared to last year

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: How do the inspection numbers you just mentioned compare to the last couple years?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So going back to 2023, we had 467 inspections.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Then 24, we had 585 inspections.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: In 2025, we had a

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: 843 inspections.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Year to date, we're at 471.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So why are the number of inspections versus last year, why have they gone significantly down?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Our inspections have been effective.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So any store that...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I couldn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Our inspection procedures have been effective.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We've visited most stores two times.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: 75% of the stores that exist in the city, we've actually been to more than once.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And we believe we've visited every store that sells these devices.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: How can you say they've been effective if we are seeing the skyrocketing numbers of these fires and fatalities?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We are not finding violations at the stores where we're able to conduct enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: As much as we did in the past.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Stores are coming into compliance.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: When we go into these stores, we're not just looking to enforce law, we're also looking to educate the people that are selling these devices.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Some people legitimately do not know that they are out of compliance with the law.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we take that opportunity to not only educate them as to what their responsibilities are,

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: as a reseller, but also let them know about fire safety.

chapters.summary: Menin says it is concerning that inspections are almost half of last year while fatalities and injuries skyrocket. Flynn attributes fires to aging batteries from the COVID-era boom that degrade from weather, salt, heat, and cold.
chapters.title: Menin challenges inspection effectiveness as fires and fatalities rise

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It just, with all due respect, it just seems very concerning that the number of inspections this year are almost half of what they were last year, and yet we are seeing the number of fatalities and injuries skyrocket this year.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Yes, the fires that we're seeing this year,

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We believe that during COVID, these devices became very, very popular here in the city.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So now we are a couple of years in, and over time, these batteries do get beat up out on our streets.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we think that they just, over the course of time, became...

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: less reliable and fail.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: They're not failing right away.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So they're subjected to the elements, the salt, the out on the roadways, the heat, the extreme heat we have here, the extreme cold, which eventually degrades the battery to the point of failure.

chapters.summary: Menin asks why the battery trade-in program was discontinued after the Council established it and the administration committed $2 million to replace unsafe devices in 2025. Flynn says it was a DOT program and defers, but Menin demands an answer by end of day.
chapters.title: Menin presses on discontinued battery trade-in program

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Well, given that the council passed legislation establishing a battery trade-in program and that the administration committed $2 million to replace more than 400 unsafe devices in 2025, why was the program discontinued?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: That is a DOT program.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I would defer to DOT for that answer.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: But we were very supportive of that program.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We were out there with DOT at some of those buyback sites.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I think it was a great program, but I would have to defer to DOT on that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So no one on this panel can answer that question of why it was, I mean, if it was a great program, why wouldn't you all push to have it continued?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we were supportive of it.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what happened about the discontinuation.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I would have to ask DOT.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, this is unbelievably troubling.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This council passed bill after bill, as I said in the opening, on this issue of these dangerous batteries.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's just pretty shocking that no one seems to know why the program was discontinued if you're saying it was effective.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I think DOT could give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I just don't have that answer, why it was discontinued.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, it's really unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm just going to be honest.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Everyone.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: knew this hearing was happening, to not have an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This is a rudimentary question about why one of the council bills was basically discontinued and something that you agree is very valuable.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Yes, that is not a...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you all to come back to these committees with an answer by the end of the day as to why.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: DOT, discontinue the program.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We will confer with DOT once we get out of here and get you an answer.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Menin asks how enforcement of sale bans on uncertified mobility devices and batteries is going. Flynn says it is going well, FDNY summonses increased to 255 from 218, and having independent authority is a force multiplier.
chapters.title: Menin asks how FDNY grades its concurrent enforcement authority

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So FDNY was given concurrent authority to enforce sale bans on uncertified mobility devices and lithium ion batteries.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: How would you say that this enforcement authority is going?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: You talked about some of this data, but how would you grade the enforcement authority and how do you feel it is going?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: It's going well.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Even though our number of inspections have decreased, our violations have actually, FDNY summons violations have increased to 255 from 218.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Having that ability to do that on our own without DCWP, I think is a huge benefit for us.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Anytime we are able to

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: It's a force multiplier.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We could have more people out on the streets conducting inspections.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I have a lot more questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to pass it to the chairs, as I know a lot of colleagues have questions as well.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks Menin, calls on Sanchez, who briefly notes her baby. Ariola asks whether the fire code currently allows criminal charges against individual e-mobility device owners. Chief Currao explains violations can lead to FDNY summonses, criminal summonses, or violation orders, but the code is written against improper storage and overstorage, not individual criminal possession.
chapters.title: Ariola takes over questioning; asks about criminal versus civil penalties in fire code

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Chair Sanchez, please.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Areola.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I just want to let folks know that that screaming baby was mine.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: My family's visiting for Thanksgiving.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So just welcome.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Love you guys.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Hola, Enneal.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Hola, Yaya.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify because Councilmember Gennaro's bill, 1189, the fire code,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: doesn't the fire code not include criminal charges currently as it stands now for individual owners of the e-mobility device?

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Chair, you were hard to hear.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Yeah, just repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Yeah, so does the existing, can the FDMY provide clarity on penalties within the fire code?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Criminal versus civil, because I think that that's an issue with this particular piece of legislation, but we just want to clarify.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Thank you for the morning, everybody.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: The fire code, if violations are written, they're written for overstoraged.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: There's a limit by which, you know, more than five kicks in additional safety parameters, such as barriers, fireproof barriers, sprinklers, things like that.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: So when we find violations, we will issue, it's really out of three.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: So one of them could be an FDNY summons, right?

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: That's something that is certified and it goes through their oath court.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Those fines actually go up progressively if someone fails to or falsely self-certifies.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Also, criminal summons, depending on the violation, more serious violations could be a criminal summons, or it could be a violation order, which kicks in a re-inspection, so we have to come back and then make sure that that issue is...

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Rectified.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Because the fire code seems silent on whether or not criminal charges are able to even be brought on the individual.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We're talking about not a brick and mortar or someone who's selling.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Speaker, I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: I didn't quite hear you.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I don't know what's wrong with my microphone.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: But because the fire code is kind of silent in the area of, maybe it's gray, in the area of can an individual be...

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Criminal charges can be brought against an individual who has an e-mobility device that is uncertified.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So because that's what we're trying to kind of flush out.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: It does not.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: And we are in code revision right now, actually.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: And we're looking at the model codes, international fire code.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: But right now, it's written against improper storage, overstores, things like that.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, so it's not criminal against an individual.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I think it's important that we understand that what we're trying to do is flush out, not so much to end an industry that we have become reliant upon since COVID and

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: put people out of business, but we do want to keep them safe and keep them alive.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks how many investigations determined a fire was caused by an uncertified, second-use, or aftermarket battery. Flynn repeats that post-fire certification determination is very difficult due to device condition.
chapters.title: Ariola asks how many investigations identify uncertified batteries

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So how many investigations determined that a fire was caused by an uncertified second-use or aftermarket battery device?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Similar to the speaker's question, it's very difficult post-fire for us to determine whether that device was certified prior to the fire due to the condition of the device

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: when we get out there to conduct our examination.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So very difficult for us to determine that and our investigators.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks if FDNY tracks types, manufacturers, or models of devices involved in fires and whether certain devices have elevated risk. Flynn says they track information non-scientifically through owner interviews and a marshal checklist, but have not identified trends.
chapters.title: Ariola asks whether FDNY tracks device types and fire risk trends

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And does the FDMY track the types, manufacturers, or models of powered mobility devices that are involved in these fires?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And if you do, are there any indications that certain types of devices contain elevated fire risk?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We do track that information.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: It's very non-scientific because we are unable to conduct a direct examination.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We gather that information mostly from interviews with the owner post-fire.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We haven't really identified any trends, though.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: The main takeaway that we've had, we developed a checklist for the marshal when they determined that there's a lithium-ion battery fire.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: They're required to complete that checklist.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: One of the items on that checklist is the brand, whether it was charging or not, what purpose the device is used for, whether it's commercial, recreational, or commuting.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Like I said, though, very non-scientific info, but we do our best to determine what the brand is.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And as I mentioned, we do communicate with the CPSC and try to share whatever info that we can so they could keep an eye out.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: national level as well.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Right.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks about circumstances like storage location, proximity to heaters, or building electrical capacity. Flynn says devices can fail if exposed to fire or extreme heat, and unsafe storage between occupants and egress is a major cause of fatalities.
chapters.title: Ariola asks what circumstances increase battery fire risk

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, and are there any circumstances or other circumstances that increase fire risk posed by powered mobility devices and lithium ion batteries?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The circumstances, like where they're stored, or are they near an electric heater, or are the electrical lines not right in the building that they're in and not

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: able to handle the voltage necessary to charge such a battery.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Did I answer my own question that time?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: You got it.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So these devices, whether they're perfect and they're not going to fail, they do pose dangers to our units and the people in that building because they can be impacted by fire.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So if the device is charged and let's say you have a candle fire, that candle fire extends to the device, that could cause the device to fail if it's subjected to extreme heat.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we want people to treat them with respect and adhere to our safety messaging, whether they have a certified product or a not certified product.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Do not have a false sense of security that this product is 100% safe.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: You should never have this device between you and your primary means of egress.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We mentioned the fire in the Bronx that just occurred.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: That was the case there.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: That moped was stored in the kitchen, which prohibited those occupants to get out.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And we see that time and time again.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And a lot of our fatalities are due to unsafe storage of these devices.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks how often the task force goes out and whether it only responds to complaints. Flynn says FDNY receives 311 complaints, tries to respond within 12 hours, has conducted 117 this year, and also proactively visits stores and adds them to fire company awareness lists.
chapters.title: Ariola asks about task force inspection frequency and proactivity

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Lithium ion battery related inspections and enforcement because I think that's what we're all kind of worried about here is that that we've seen a downturn in inspections and an uptick in fires so

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I know that the speaker spent time on this, but I think there's not enough time that can be spent on this.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We really do need to amp up the task force that you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So my question is, how many times does the task force go out, and does it only go out when a complaint is made, or you have a regular, you know, do you go out and just spot check?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Stores that are selling these types of devices.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: All of the above.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we do receive 311 complaints for lithium ion concerns.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I can just give you the 311 stats.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So, so far this year on 311 complaints, we've had 117.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And we try to get out there within 12 hours to conduct those inspections related to lithium ion.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we have conducted 117, but we are also proactive.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We make sure that we're aware of all these stores that are in our city.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We want the fire companies to be aware of it as well.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we make sure that that goes on to what we call SIDS.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So the fire company is aware of it, the existence of that danger there.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we do both.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We go out on our own.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We try to identify all of these locations to conduct inspections.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We believe that we've visited every store that we can find.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And 75% of these stores we visited more than one time.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Even though our number of fires has risen dramatically from last year, our number of structural fires has actually gone down.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We have 160 structural fires year to date compared to 100 and 100.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Actually, one second.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Let me just give you that number.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So structurally, we have 160.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Last year, at this time, we had 167 structural fires.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: That means fires that are inside your residence.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Those are the fires that we're most concerned with.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Those are the fires that hurt our residents and kill our residents.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we do believe that our messaging is effective, getting people to keep these devices outside, keep and store them outside, as opposed to leaving them in your apartment.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: However,

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: However, we do understand that that's not always possible for a majority of our residents here in the city in such a cramped space.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So therefore, we develop safety messaging, how best to utilize these inside your apartment.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Use a certified charger with a certified battery.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: If you have a spare room, keep it in the spare room and close the door.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Keep the battery in the bathroom and close the door if that's what you absolutely have to do.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We don't want these inside ever, but we do sympathize with the need for some people to keep them inside.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We just want to use them as safe as possible.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks how FDNY contains or disposes of confiscated e-mobility devices and batteries. Flynn says FDNY does not seize batteries; hazmat units collect and make them safe in barrels with cell-block material, then DEP and sanitation collect them.
chapters.title: Ariola asks how FDNY stores and disposes of confiscated batteries

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Right, which then again points back to the speaker's point of a very important program of battery exchange, which was no longer funded.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So you mentioned in your testimony, Commissioner, that there really isn't a cabinet yet that you have learned that can contain these fires.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So how– I have two questions.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So–

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: storage and battery charging cabinets come under fire code 309.3.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: But I wonder, once you do go in and you take these batteries or you confiscate e-mobility devices and then you put them into your own warehouse or such, how are you protecting

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: your facility from any of those batteries from combusting, even because they can combust without charge.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: as the first deputy commissioner testified to.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So how are you containing it when you're taking those bikes or you're taking those, or how are you disposing of those batteries?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we do not seize any batteries for the fire department.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We work along with DEP and sanitation for mitigation.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Our hazmat units do come out and they collect them.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: They make them safe.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: They put them in barrels with cell block material that would limit their ability to spread.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we do not take them.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: That's done in conjunction with DEP and sanitation.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: But you oversee their...

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: How they're maintained.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We mitigate the matacene.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So our hazmat units come out.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: This has actually increased the workload of our hazmat units exponentially, this proliferation of these battery fires.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So they come out.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: They're very well trained in this at this point.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: They wear their full PPE when they collect these cells.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We want to make sure we collect every single cell that is in that apartment because each cell has its own ability to start a fire.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: As I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Again and again.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: They can be shot 60 feet across a room.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: For our marshals, it makes their investigation very difficult because in the past, if you saw two separate fires, that would necessarily mean, ordinarily mean that it was an incendiary fire.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: But here, we have the potential for small fires throughout the apartment due to individual cells.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: being expelled from the device.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So some of these batteries, these sleeves of batteries, they can have hundreds of these cells in there.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So hazmat is tasked with trying to identify every cell that we can find and put them in a container to stop a secondary fire.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we container them, we bring them out to the street, make them safe,

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: and then we notify sanitation or DEP to come collect them.

chapters.summary: Bonsignore says the DOT pilot was scheduled for two years and completed in 2025, which is why it ended. Menin says if it was working, the agency could renew it without Council legislation.
chapters.title: Commissioner Bonsignore provides answer on DOT trade-in pilot

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Chair Ariel, if you wouldn't mind, I have, we were able to get an answer for the DOT pilot.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Oh, wonderful.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So the DOT pilot was scheduled for a two-year pilot and was completed in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: That's how long the council included it in the pilot.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So it was concluded in 2025, which is why it ended.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, thank you for that data, but if it's working, why wouldn't it continue?

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: That's something we could follow up on.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We are supportive of the trade-in program, so we'll have to see.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Through DOT, what can happen through the council, I don't have an answer for that.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: But that's the answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Well, I mean, just to be clear, you don't need council legislation to do the buy.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, the DOT agency commissioner can make that decision.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: You don't need us to do it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I would just say if there's a program that's working,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It shouldn't be that the program expires and no one thinks, well, why don't we then just renew it?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: You don't need us to renew it.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We'll be happy to follow.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Bonsignore clarifies her earlier comment referred to containers and bags for workers, not storage cabinets. She says no bag has withstood a lithium-ion battery fire, but cabinets are a developing technology.
chapters.title: Bonsignore clarifies fireproof bags versus storage cabinets

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And just one other point.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So when I was talking about the product before, I was talking about the containers or the bags, not so much the storage

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: units, but the containers and the bags that were proposed to give to the workers to put their batteries in.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We have not seen any product that has been able to withstand a lithium ion.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Battery fire.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: The cabinets, we could speak more about the cabinets if you like.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Yeah, I would like to know more about the cabinets because we need to be able to give people who are using these mobility devices and the lithium ion batteries, and we want them to be certified, but we also want them to be safe in storing them and also secure.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I understand why they want to take it into their apartment, and I'm sure they're very costly, so they don't want to leave them outside and such.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So, I mean, one of the pieces of legislation speaks to that.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So if we can get cabinetry that will contain or mitigate the extent of the fire that we're seeing now, then that would be great.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We share your desire wholeheartedly.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We want these batteries to be outside, stored outside, charged outside, and cabinets will help that.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: But it is still a developing technology, so we have to make sure that the cabinets are also safe.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And I think that's where we are in the process now.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Chief Correa does this full time, so he's happy to talk a little bit more about that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Great, thank you.

chapters.summary: Currao says FDNY has certified six cabinet models at 22 sites using a letter of no objection process, is phasing into UL 1487, and works with manufacturers on safe installation, clearances, site reviews, and inspections.
chapters.title: Chief Currao describes certified battery cabinet program

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Yes, Chair, we currently have six models that have been certified.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: We use a letter of no objection process because we had to really come up with a process to make sure that the full-scale testing of these cabinets was analyzed to make sure that they were safe for deployment on the streets.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: We have six different models out there, 22 different sites across the city.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: We put that in place before the Underwriters Laboratory standard 1487 was developed, which came out in the beginning of 2025.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: We're phasing into that now where all new cabinets have to meet that standard because it's even safer.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: But we leaned into it very early on.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: We worked.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: We had a task force with a lot of our manufacturers to hear them out, to work on collaborative solutions.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: In fact, a lot of those manufacturers were also on the Underwriters Laboratory Committee that developed those standards.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: So we've been working really for years on it, as well as providing website guidance on safe installation, on maintaining clearances from fire escapes and fire hydrants and things like that.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: We also do site reviews when they want to put them in, as well as inspections.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: So what's really important about these battery cabinet site areas, and we fully support the effort to make it.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: make sure that they're out there.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: It supports the theme of outdoor storage, but they have to be continually maintained too.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: That's obviously really important to the overall mission.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: So just wanted to add some additional.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks why the administration is pushing outdoor storage kiosks and facilities funding to 2028 when they are needed now. Currao points to a nearby delivery hub with charging, repair, and guidance as a positive model.
chapters.title: Ariola criticizes timeline pushing outdoor storage funding to 2028

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I appreciate that because it makes, it gives me another question, which is why then is the administration pushing that out to 2028?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Instead, you know, the outdoor storage kiosks and facilities and things of that nature, they're pushing the funding out to 2028.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We need them now.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: It's not for you to answer.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I just don't understand why we're not addressing it now, and it would go to 2028.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Chair, I just wanted to mention, like, right outside, we have a really good example of collaboration with one of our manufacturers, and the delivery is the hub that not only has charging, but also minor repair and also guidance for the delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: So I think that's, like, a really positive model that we have right in the city.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: We can continue to replicate and work with our interagency partners as well as our cabinet installers and manufacturers.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Yeah, but the timeline has been pushed to 2028.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: That's the thing.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We should be seeing more.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: More centers like that.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks whether FDNY goes door-to-door in areas with mobility devices, hands out literature in multiple languages, and follows up. Flynn describes the eSafety Task Force focusing on commercial establishments and complaints, informational materials, tenant guides, and fdmysmart.org.
chapters.title: Ariola asks how FDNY conducts door-to-door education and follow-up

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So I want to go back to the task force.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: When the FDMY does the door-to-door team, is it a door-to-door task force?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Do you go out?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Do you knock on doors in areas where,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You would think that people have mobility devices and just hand out literature to educate them in different languages

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: to how to possibly store safely or to look to see whether or not the battery has a certified stamp on it.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: How do you follow up?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Is it by mail or email?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So what's the whole process, if you could walk us through it?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I think these are a couple of things.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We have the eSafety Task Force, which really focuses on commercial establishments going out there at point of sale to enforce that local law 39.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So that's what the eSafety Task Force focuses on, as well as following up on complaints.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Sometimes we get complaints from residential buildings where there's storage in the public area.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we'll go out there and try to enforce that, do any enforcement that is warranted and conduct inspections there.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We do give informational materials every time we go out and inspect these locations to the commercial establishments.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And we also, as mentioned in the commissioner's testimony, in the tenant guide that we hand out, that does have lithium ion safety messaging in there as well, as well as our own website, fdmysmart.org.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We have constant safety messaging on lithium ion batteries as well as other fire safety concerns.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We've launched a lithium ion safety messaging campaign.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: It's going to run for five weeks.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: With the help of the FDNY Foundation to fund it.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We've done campaigns similar in the past where we had $750,000 to conduct with your mind safety messaging.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And we think that made a difference.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: As mentioned last year, we had one fire fatality due to these devices.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Our campaign concluded, of course.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And this year we've had nine.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We would love to continue to support as much safety messaging as possible with extra funding for that.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: As I mentioned, right now we're relying on our fire foundation to fund our current campaign.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: But any dedicated items for us to do fire safety education, not just in the lithium ion battery front, but for all fire safety concerns.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And do you also go to like third party like Uber or any of the other Uber Eats, DoorDash?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Do you also have conversations with those companies?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We have had many conversations with those companies to try to encourage them to treat their employees with respect.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I think they could probably be doing more in that regard as well.

chapters.summary: Bonsignore says the problem will grow with more batteries and bikes, education is critical, and FDNY relies on its foundation for campaigns. She cites 3,242 fire safety presentations reaching 433,000 people and 970 school events reaching over 100,000 kids, and proposes a weekly Fire Safety Friday.
chapters.title: Bonsignore calls for sustained education funding and Fire Safety Friday

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I would add, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: You know, I do think we understand how big a problem this is, but this is a technology that more and more people are now starting to engage in.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So there will be more and more batteries, more and more bikes, more and more problems.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And part of...

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Really setting our city up for success is education.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Like we have to teach.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: people how to use these devices, how to be safe, and not only with lithium ion batteries, but with all fire safety.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I mean, it's a critical point to keeping people safe.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We have millions of people in this city that need to hear this messaging over and over again.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: To have maybe a dedicated funding line to provide, you know, constant and continuous education would be helpful for us because we do rely heavily on our foundation to try to get some of that funding.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: But I will say, like, even just this year, we've done 3,242.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Fire safety presentations, which had an audience of 433,000 people.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We've done 970 school events, so we're even getting into schools to get the kids up on fire safety, over 100,000 kids that have been educated.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And I think that is really part of what we need to continue to keep our eyes on, not only the legislative end, but also how do we work together to educate the city, not just 400,000 people or 100,000 people,

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: but 8.5 million people.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And that is the stuff that...

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I will continue to advocate for it, and I will ask for everybody's help.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Honestly, if we could have a Fire Safety Friday every week, where every single person, every elected, everybody...

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: have

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: as an audience with the public, put some of our tips out there.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: The news, the radios, the influencers, the electeds, everybody did Fire Safety Friday.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I think people would get the message quicker than we can do with our staff and our budget.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So I think we have to accept that

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: This is a changing technology, and it is putting us in a very difficult place as it emerges and standards start to become something that will make it safer.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: But education is by far, I think, one of the most important things we can do.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And we need to do this in every language, with every community, and we are happy to work with anybody to do it.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I encourage you to have, you know, Fire Safety Friday, where you can go to fdmysmart.org for tips.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We have it all up there.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We have resources.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Share it.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Talk about it.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Do PSAs with us.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Anything that we can do to teach people, because it is, you know, ultimately behind closed doors.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So we need people to be armed with the proper information.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks Bonsignore and turns to HPD. She asks whether HPD inspects for e-bike storage and charging in dwellings and shared spaces and distributes multilingual lithium-ion battery information. Josh Cucchiarella says HPD does not currently inspect for e-bikes or batteries but provides best-practice information and translations in 10 languages. Ariola criticizes the lack of direct inspections and outreach.
chapters.title: Ariola asks HPD about e-bike inspections and multilingual outreach

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And I certainly will be partaking.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You can count on me.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So I just have two questions for HPD, and then I'm going to yield to Chair Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So for HPD.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: To what extent does HPD

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: currently inspect for e-bike storage and charging in their residential dwellings, hallways, or other shared spaces?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And do you currently distribute to your tenants in various languages that they could understand about information on lithium-ion batteries?

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: So we do not currently inspect for e-bikes or lithium ion batteries during our inspections.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: We do, however, provide tenants with information during each inspection about associated best practices.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: While the entire pamphlet that we provide tenants is not translated, there are translations in 10 different languages that direct tenants to our website where the entire pamphlet is translated into the 10 languages.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: In addition, we have information on our website about best practices associated with lithium ion battery use.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, so I'm going to say right off the bat, you're not reaching your audience at their level.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You need to do inspections.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You need to make sure because people are dying in your buildings.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And so you need to have...

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Piece of paper that is in other languages that you can hand to the tenant, not asking them, do you have a bike inside, how many, but

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Saying, if you do.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: This could happen.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: This is how you can prevent it in their own language so they can understand it.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Because if we're not reaching them at their level, then we're not reaching them at all.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And that's why we're having the issues we're having in HPD-run buildings.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: To say that you don't inspect for e-mobility devices, I live in a co-op.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I have to keep the bicycle in an area on the main floor.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: It should be expected.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: That's what you should be looking for.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And I find that HPD does not do their due diligence in those areas.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And that's why tenants are being put at risk.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I mean, I can't imagine, is the city aware of the extent of which you're not doing outreach the way you should?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Is the administration aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Like, you know, why aren't you doing it?

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: I hear you.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: And actually, if I can just qualify my answer somewhat.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: So during all of our inspections, we are looking at a host of different potential fire safety issues, right?

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: So in addition to the self-closing door inspections that we conduct in every apartment when we enter one, we're also looking at both smoke and carbon monoxide detectors to make sure that they're installed and in operation when we're inspecting.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: As of January 1st, we will also include gas detectors.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: We're also looking to make sure that egress is adequate from apartments and from buildings generally in the common areas.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: So while we do not look specifically for e-bikes or lithium-ion batteries, if we find encumbered egress, we will cite those conditions.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Right, but they have to be, when you're going in and you're inspecting and you're seeing that and it is encumbering egress, they have to have something that you could give to them for outreach so that they could know

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: why they shouldn't be at the point of entry and what could possibly happen.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I now yield to Chair Sanchez.

chapters.summary: Ariola yields to Sanchez and notes Councilmember Lincoln Restler has joined. Sanchez notes the West Bronx has 40% of Bronx fires, then asks what investigative steps FDNY takes to determine if a fire was caused by a lithium-ion battery or micromobility device. Flynn explains marshals use the scientific method, dig out scenes, interview occupants, and look for expelled cells, but do not investigate every fire.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks FDNY to walk through fire marshal investigations

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And note that we've been joined by Council Member Lincoln Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair, and good morning again.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: You know, I want to start my questions with the reality.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: You know, for us in the West Bronx, we have 40% of the Bronx's fires.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We are nowhere near 40% of the Bronx's population.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And then we know that the Bronx faces a higher rate of fire than the other boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And so, you know, that's a grounding statistic to the truths that we've been laying out during today's hearing of all of the New Yorkers that we are losing and, you know, what keeps me up at night and I know my team as well.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So my first question is, after a fire occurs, what investigative steps does FDNY undertake to determine that a fire was caused by a lithium-ion battery, a micromobility device, or a different cause?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Can you walk us through specifically what that fire marshal investigation does look like?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I know the speaker and the chair have already asked about how you determine whether a battery was UL certified or not, understanding that the sticker might get corroded.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Is that something that the fire marshal looks at during the investigation?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And then I'll continue from there.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, certainly.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And I had the pleasure of joining you up at your office to conduct some fire safety.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: in the area as well and thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I think it was very, very effective.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: In my past role prior to this job, I was the chief fire marshal.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So I'm very familiar with the process when it comes to the fire investigations.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We do not know immediately what the cause is.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we're not investigating as a lithium ion battery fire.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: The firefighters go and they extinguish

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Every fire in the same way.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We use copious amounts of water to extinguish the fire.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Firefighters do not know what type of fire they're fighting when they arrive at a fire scene, of course.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Our marshals always use the same approach when they're conducting a fire investigation.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We go and examine the scene.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We call digging it out.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We dig out the room, make sure that we get all the contents out there, look for any patterns that are either suspicious or would help us identify the location where the fire started, try to identify a heat source that would have been in that area

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: that we can try to find remnants of.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Sometimes if it is a battery, as I mentioned earlier, we will find those expelled cells in the room, and there's many of those cells that are in those packs.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I don't think most people realize that sleeve contains hundreds, possibly, of these little batteries, that every one of them has the full capacity to start a fire on its own.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: It has the fuel, it has the heat source, everything that's needed to start a fire is in each one of those cells.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So it would be expelled and we'd identify

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: where those cells are, try to work with hazmat to collect as many as possible.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: But all fire investigations start at the same point, and we go through the same process to determine the cause of the fire.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We use the scientific method.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We need to be able to recreate that investigation.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: It's very difficult for a fire marshal to determine what the cause of a fire is due to the scene as we find it when we get there.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Obviously, the fire causes a tremendous amount of damage.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Fire extinguishment causes a tremendous amount of damage.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we work with the firefighters.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We do interviews.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: What did you see when you got here?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Where was this?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We try to work with the occupant also to recreate the room.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: What did the room look like before the fire?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: What was where?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Where was the bed?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Where was the nightstand?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Did you charge something here?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we do a lot of interviews and examination.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So it's an investigation as well as an examination to determine the cause.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: The fire marshals conduct about 5,000 fire investigations a year.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: 2,000 of those investigations are car fires.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we record all car fires.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: There is a threshold for the fire marshals to conduct an examination.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: The standard would be an all-hands fire, which is a significant fire for the department.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: That would trigger an automatic response by the marshals.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Or if the chief requests us out there, if we believe there's criminality.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So there is a criteria for an investigation, but marshals do not investigate every

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: single fire as we had a big number of fires obviously in the city.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Marshals do not investigate all fires.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Marshals have approximately 140 marshals in the city to conduct 5,000 fire investigations.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we really need to triage.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Is it 140?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: About 140.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And so just drilling in on the lithium ion battery, so there's not during, not after the investigation, there's no way for the fire department to determine whether a battery or the sleeve was to code?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Well, currently the code would not prohibit a non-certified device to be in your apartment, so that would not really be a violation of the code.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: But just for our own information, we do our best to determine what brand the battery was, what brand the bike was, what brand the charger was.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Because there is a relationship between the charger and the battery.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We want to make sure that the battery management system will function in conjunction with that battery.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So not only does the battery need to be a high quality battery, we need high quality chargers as well.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether lithium-ion battery fires are caused by overheating, poor quality, brand trends, or interaction with older building electrical systems.
