Flynn says they have not determined building electrical issues leading to battery failure; battery quality and condition are the main factors.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks whether battery failures relate to building electrical issues

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And that's exactly what I was trying to understand because there is, you know, the increasing role that lithium-ion batteries is playing in fires across our city,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: but then there's also that second leading cause of fires in our city being the old, you know, the electrical systems within properties.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So I suppose to be as specific as I can, I'm trying to understand whether

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: their lithium ion batteries are, whether the department thinks that lithium ion batteries are leading to the fires because they are overheating, exploding, poor quality, there's any trends with brands or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And what is the connection between, you know, whether the battery was plugged into a building, you know, that has older systems, maybe there was, you know, a short circuit, caused a spark, something like that.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We haven't determined any building electrical issues that would lead to the battery failing on its own.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: It's more of the quality of the battery, the state of the battery.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: As I mentioned, a good battery can become a bad battery if it's beat up and the casing is broken.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We beat up our batteries and our devices here in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We have extreme seasons here.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So the salt, you can see the roadway, how bad the roadway gets beat up.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So that's the same for the batteries.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And some of these people that utilize the batteries use this for their livelihood, and they work really long hours really hard.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And we respect them, and we want to support them in any way possible.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: But we want to make sure they're safe and their families are safe, at the same time supporting their need for these devices.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how FDNY and HPD measure whether tabling, media, and paid advertising work. Bonsignore says it is hard to quantify prevented fires but more education means fewer fires; she cites a translation app covering 28 languages and school outreach. Flynn highlights Get Alarmed NYC smoke detector installations. Currao notes annual fire safety bulletins in 13 languages.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks agencies how they measure outreach effectiveness

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Deputy Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So my next question is following up on Chair's Areola line of questioning and discussion with HPD.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But really, really for all of you, I mean, there are multiple city agencies involved in trying to educate the public and prevent

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: event fires from happening in the city.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: You know, I think I have FDNY at every single community event that we have.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you for always showing up.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I think I have about a billion of those fire prevention books in my office, and we take them everywhere that we can.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But how do you measure effectiveness?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How do you judge whether...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Tabling or this media outlet or this paid, you know, out advertising is working and is reaching folks.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How are you working to improve that outreach?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All of you, actually, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: HPD can start, maybe FDNY can.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I'll start us off if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So, you know, it's really about the blitz.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Like, it's not so much about the numbers.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: It's hard to qualify how many fires don't happen because of education.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: But the more education that we give, the less fires we see.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: But there's no way to actually put a number that we prevented 100 fires because of our education.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: But we do know that the education works.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So it's about really flooding the area in different types of media.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So some of it is the books that you have.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Some of it is a table, and we do that particularly after a fatal fire.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We put resources in that area so they can talk to everybody.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We've just developed an app that is a translation app.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So it is a conversational translation app so that we can talk to anybody in their language.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I think it translates 28 languages at this point.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We're still trying to expand that.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We leave materials in the buildings.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We go up and down and leave it on doors.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We go to schools.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We go to everywhere.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So the easy answer is...

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I don't have a number as to how you measure that it's working.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We just know the more education that we give them, the less fires we see.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And especially when it comes to the kids, I think, you know, the kids are an important piece of this equation here because they absorb so easily.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And they really connect with fire safety.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So, you know, we're putting a lot of efforts in going into the schools, and I think that's important for our immigrant families as well.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: When the kids come home, they can translate and kind of look for some of the things that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I'll turn it over to H.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Can I just add one thing?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I'd like to just highlight another program that we support, and it's Get Alarmed NYC.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: That is a smoke detector program.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So that gives people an option to request smoke detector installations in conjunction with the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we go out there, and we will install.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Those smoke detectors in your house.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: If you don't have a smoke detector, an operational smoke detector in your house, please reach out, call 311 to request an installation, and we will go out there free of charge and install smoke detectors in your home.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Councilwoman, oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: I just wanted to add to that.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: That is built into our code, so an annual fire safety bulletin.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: And it's a great opportunity to, because that's really through the building owners themselves, and it covers a whole host of fire safety hazards.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: But that's where we really need the assistance of building management, building ownership, to make sure that those bulletins and guides are getting to the residents.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: It provides a lot of information about what to do in a fire, and it's in multiple languages, 13 different languages.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: So just wanted to add.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And we do look at how many people we actually have touched in the audience, which is really the number that we kind of use as a guide.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: The more people, like I said, the more people, the better.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So we have not only the fire safety education out there, but we also have our CPR unit out there.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And this is a constant everyday event.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So we're trying to train as many people as possible.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Commissioner, if you have those numbers for how many folks FDNY's outreach efforts reached this year, that would be great.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Yeah, I think I actually just talked a little bit about it before.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We had over 433...

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Thousand people got fire safety education and then we had over a hundred and nine thousand school kids that got fire safety education that was this year

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how FDNY shares data with DOB and HPD and whether it informs policymaking like Article 11. Cucchiarella says agencies remain in contact and a dashboard could be great if manageable. Bonsignore says FDNY already publishes NYC Open Data but needs it more digestible, and she has discussed electrical systems with Commissioner Levy.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks HPD about interagency coordination and fire dashboard

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: HPD, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: So I think in answer to your question, Council Member, there's a couple of different ways success can be measured.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: I think definitely a review of data.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: data over a number of different years could potentially bear out some information about the success of the efforts being made to educate New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: But in addition to that, I think some of the success can be measured somewhat anecdotally.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: And I'll cite an example from just this past week.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: I attended a meeting with tenants at 1512 Townsend Avenue in the Bronx, and I presented information about our inspection procedures.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: And I ran through all of the nine points, and we really honed in on fire safety aspects.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: And the tenant organizer...

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: Essentially indicated to me that they already know all of that and she was more interested in the new stuff we're doing.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: And so what I think that shows is that the education campaigns made over time about things like self-closing doors and smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors, has been effective.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Sticking with HPD, this is something that I feel like I've been bringing up in every hearing, budget hearings and et cetera, with HPD is about the coordination, right?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So my bill intro 1174 would create a dashboard, a public-facing dashboard.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you for your feedback, Commissioner, on ways that that bill could be stronger.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But the idea is NYPD has CompStat.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The public knows what's going on.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: know where it's going on, and the idea is to have that kind of information available to the public, you know, to keep this issue

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: at the forefront of their minds, but also to be pushing, to encourage the public to push lawmakers, policymakers, to do better in terms of fire prevention.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And so my question here is about

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: interagency coordination.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I've had several conversations with Commissioner Levy in the beginning of the year when we were seeing that there was going to be, it was going to be a difficult year with fires.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And when I mentioned to her that electrical systems and electrical reasons were

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: top of the list, she was surprised, right?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And so I know that conversations have evolved since then, but how does FDNY share data with Department of Buildings, HPD, and how does that information inform policymaking

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: in areas like, for instance, Article 11, where the city is giving financial incentives to preserve buildings, are we preserving them according to the information that we get from FDNY about the causes of fires?

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: So what I'll say in terms of the ongoing coordination between our agency, specifically HPDF, DNY, and DOB, is

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: we remain in pretty consistent contact with our sister agencies, and we continually look for new ways to address underlying electrical conditions that potentially cause fires.

utterances.speaker: Josh Cucchiarella
utterances.text: I think as the fire commissioner mentioned earlier, a dashboard like you described in the bill is potentially a great idea provided it's rolled out in a manageable way.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I would add, like, we like the idea of being transparent, getting that out there.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We actually do put information out through NYC Open Data, but we need to make it more digestible, I think.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: That's what you're trying to accomplish here.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And I will just tell you on a side note that Commissioner Levy and I have already had a conversation about...

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: The electrical systems in buildings.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So I know that she is aware and we are scheduled to meet at the fire department to discuss it further.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: That's amazing.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: It's really great to hear.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And I know my colleagues have questions.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about the DOT battery charging pilot and whether it will continue. Chief Currao says FDNY meets with DOT every two weeks, helped write requirements, and understands the pilot will be extended.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about DOT battery charging pilot status

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So just two more from me.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: DOT is not here, but we did, I believe, send a question about the battery charging pilot.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I've been in communication with certain leaders in certain parts of my district who

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: have been trying to get battery charging stations outside of their buildings to keep those batteries outside.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Wondering if you have any information about the status of that pilot and whether it's going to continue.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Councilwoman, is that the Revical Consent Program?

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Is that through DOT?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Yeah, so we keep in constant communication with DOT.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: We meet with them actually every two weeks.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: We helped write and build a lot of the requirements that need to be achieved and also with DOB.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: And as far as the pilot itself, my understanding from our very recent discussions is that that will be extended.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: And we are looking for, you know, really to try to open up the array of outside battery charging opportunities, whether that's through revical consent or they use, you know, private property.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: You know, we want to support all those different avenues to get to outside charging.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez says FDNY and she shared confusion on criminal versus civil penalties for possession, noting fire code penalties are civil under 3 RCNY 109-03. Bonsignore says FDNY worries about penalizing ordinary people who may not know their device is uncertified and wants to focus on point of sale.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks clarification on Intro 1189 criminal versus civil penalties

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: A point of clarification on Intro 1189.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Our council advised us that FDNY and I actually shared the confusion on criminal versus civil penalties for possession.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Fire code penalties are established by 3 RCNY 109-03, which includes civil penalties.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Why is it that FDNY came to the conclusion that the implementation of Intro 1189 would carry criminal penalties for possession?

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Yeah, I believe our interest here is that, you know, there are a lot of individuals that have these things that may not even know that they are not certified.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And we're worried about penalizing normal people, whether it be civil or criminal.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We do think that we just need to focus on the point of sale.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: That's where they're coming from.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Those are the folks that are selling these things.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Sometimes I would imagine they'd be under the guise of they're legal and certified.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So I think our concern is that, is that we don't want to penalize an average everyday person who may not even know that they have a battery that's not certified.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And I agree with you, as I said in my opening remarks, but I will now turn it back to the chair.

chapters.summary: Ariola says users have had three years to know batteries need certification, asks whether FDNY opposes criminal penalties and whether civil penalties are acceptable. Bonsignore says FDNY is worried about penalizing individuals civilly or criminally and wants to focus on the source. Ariola says hearings help amend bill language.
chapters.title: Ariola and Bonsignore discuss penalties and amending Intro 1189

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So just on that issue, they've had three years to know that the batteries needed to be certified.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So they had advance notice, and that's why I'm focusing so much on education and outreach in different languages and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: But would you...

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Are you saying that you don't support a criminal?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: a criminal penalty, right?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Which this bill, as I read it, does not on the individual have a criminal penalty for the individual, but the civil portion, that would be something that you would support or?

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I think we're worried about penalizing someone either in a civil or criminal arena.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I think, you know, our focus really has to be at the root of where these things are coming from.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So we're not looking, as of right now, the way it's written, we're not looking to penalize an individual.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I would agree.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And I think that that's why we have these hearings, so that we can talk about what the language of a bill is and talk about what we can amend in these bills and how we can make these bills work for everyone so that we have public safety.

chapters.summary: Zhuang thanks FDNY for saving two lives in Sunset Park, notes many residents were subleasing or in informal housing, and asks how fire safety information reaches them. Bonsignore says FDNY must work with community leaders and trusted partners, and clarifies no cause determination has been made in the Sunset Park fire.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks how fire safety info reaches informal housing residents

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Councilmember Zhuang, you have questions?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And I want to thank Commissioner and also firefighters who saved two lives in my district in the Sunset Park fire.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: But more than just the house had a fire, many people impacted by the Sunset Park fire in my district.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: They were subleasing their apartment or living in informal housing arrangement.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How do you make sure the fire safety information reaches those residents?

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I could start us off, and then we can turn it over to the chief of department.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I just want to make just a note on the Sunset Park fire.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: It was absolutely tragic, and our hearts are broken over this.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I know the community is very impacted by that loss, as all the fatalities in our fires have been.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: It's very difficult for...

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: First responders as well because you know we want we want to save lives we want people to be okay and it's just so so terrible but on a sense of park fire we're getting a lot of inquiries

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: and assumptions that the cause is the battery and we I just want to be clear we have made no determination here we should not assume anything until an actual

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: determination has been made based on the investigation.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So I just want to make sure we're speaking the same language here.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And then as far as the, you know, getting the information out, I think it's really important that we work with the community leaders,

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: that we work with the electeds, that we work with all the people that are really just like tied into the community.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I think there may be some

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: concern, right?

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: When people start coming around in uniform, we start talking about what

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: you should and should not do, maybe people get a little nervous.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And I think when we partner with people that they trust, when we partner with the community leaders, we can be much more effective together.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So I would say that would be something we would be very interested in doing.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We will do that in any community.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: On any day at any time.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And I think it's going to take that in order to get that information into the, you know, every corner of our communities.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I'll turn it over to Chief of Department.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And thank you for recognizing the firefighters at the Sunset Park fire that

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: It was a very tragic night, but they did rescue two people from the rear of that building that were trapped behind window bars with fire and smoke coming behind them.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Concerning the sharing of information, excuse me one second.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: The landlords also have a responsibility when people sign a lease to share the information about the type of building that they're in, whether it's a fire-resistant building or a

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: non-fireproof building, and the actions that they should take during a fire.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And that should be built into the lease.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks whether window bars were the issue in Sunset Park and whether FDNY inspected nearby window bars. Chief Esposito says firefighters removed window bars to rescue two people, window bars are not illegal, and FDNY records their presence for responder awareness but does not issue violations.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about window bars and inspections after Sunset Park

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Is the window bar the issue in that event in Sunset Park, the fire?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: There were window bars on the rear of the building with people trapped behind them, and our firefighters had to remove those window bars to get those people out.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: But the second floor did not have window bar.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Yeah, but, right, those people were not at the windows, though, from the second floor.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So no one able to save the second floor.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And also, you said about the window bar issue.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Did you guys go back to the same area to inspect the window bars around?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: in the neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: No, the window bars are not illegal.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: The window bar is not legal.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: They're not illegal.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: They're not illegal.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Is any window bar an issue in the Sunset Park area?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Did you guys go back to inspect?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: That's my question.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We would inspect to look to put that on our data so that our firefighters, when they respond to that address, might know that there are window bars.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: But it's not something we inspect and write a violation for because it's not illegal.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: It's not a violation.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks how often FDNY inspects Sunset Park e-bike vendors and whether the city can invest in fireproof bags for delivery workers. Esposito says FDNY has visited all bike stores and will provide dates. He says bags designed to keep fire out are different from bags meant to contain a battery fire, and FDNY testing has not found such bags to work.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about e-bike vendor inspections and fireproof bags

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And I'll also go back to the e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: This is not the first time.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I'm not saying the cause of that fire in Sunset Park is e-bike issue, but how often you guys go to Sunset Park area to inspect the vendors sell e-bikes?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: When is the last time you go back to that area to inspect?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We can get that, but we've been to all the bike stores throughout the city that sell e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And we'll get you the date if we can try to find the dates.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Yeah, I'd like to see the date.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And also the other is a brainstorm question.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: You know, I have a bag at home.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: It's a fireproof bag to put a passport.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: the other important document in.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Do we able to have some type of bag for the, like a deliver worker, after they finish their work, they can put their battery in?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Is that something New York City can invest?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And I believe that's one of the,

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: one of the pieces of proposed legislation, the problem is we're not aware that that exists.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: The bag that you're putting your documents in is to keep the fire out.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: The bag that we're looking to put batteries in is to keep the fire in the bag.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And we're not sure that anything exists like that.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We have, in the past couple of years, we have done tests at the fire academy, and people have suggested that these bags would work, and our testing proved otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Ariola calls on Restler. Restler thanks FDNY, says outdoor charging cabinets and battery swap services are promising, and asks if FDNY supports expansion and what steps streamline permitting while maintaining safety. Currao describes the letter of no objection process, site surveys, and an approximately eight-week review timeline.
chapters.title: Restler asks about expanding battery swap cabinets and permitting

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Council Member Feliz.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Oh, sure.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Councilmember Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I got double booked or quadruple booked as these things go.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But we really appreciate the leadership of the fire department, the courage and heroism of our firefighters for keeping New Yorkers safe.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And just want to express my deep and profound gratitude to the men and women of the fire department and the work you do every day.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Like my esteemed co-chairs this morning and my colleagues, I am deeply concerned about the growing rise of residential fires from lithium-ion batteries.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I think one of the most promising solutions are these outdoor charging cabinets through battery swap services.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Does the fire department support expansion of these battery swap services, and what steps have been taken to streamline the permitting and approval process while maintaining safety?

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Councilman.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: So we've been really engaged with this really for years in supporting outdoor charging and battery cabinet installation.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: We started with the letter of no objection process, which was a

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: really comprehensive process to make sure that testing, full-scale testing that is done through underwriters laboratory is analyzed

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: before we issued a letter of no objection so that that cabinet can be used safely in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: We created a process where applicants can

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: submit a site survey.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: It's really a pretty basic survey, but it gives us all the information we need to know that that particular battery cabinet siting area is safe.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Can you share an average timeline that it takes FDNY to review applications for battery swap cabinets?

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: It's approximately eight weeks, and the reason for that is it's done through our district offices that have tens of thousands of permit inspections as well, so it's not the only thing that they do.

chapters.summary: Restler says operators report nine months and $10,000 costs; Currao says that is inaccurate and offers to provide data. They discuss separate teams for large energy storage systems and smaller battery cabinets, and Currao says district offices can maintain the two-month turnaround.
chapters.title: Restler questions nine-month, $10,000 permitting claims and asks for data

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We've heard from operators that it can take nine months and cost $10,000.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You think that's inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: That is inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is there data that you can share with our office so that we can better understand how you've been able to streamline the process and show how long it's taken to issue permits?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: For applicants?

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: So let me just answer your question one at a time.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: So one of the things is that we need the help of industry, right?

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: So we've had applications that have suggested that outdoor battery cabinets, we're not talking about large-scale energy storage systems, under fire escapes, on construction sites.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: We also have a standing rule that if they are not in compliance with DOB, we will not issue them that site approval.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: So because we work very, very closely on that.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: If you're talking about, and we can provide you data on that, no problem.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: As well as the energy storage systems, the larger systems, we can provide data for that too.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: That's a much more involved process because that's a bigger system that's a lot more complicated to our technology.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I guess to that point, is it the same teams?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is it your same team that's reviewing those applications for the large battery storage systems as for the smaller battery swap cabinets?

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: So the battery storage systems, the large ones, is through our technology management unit.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: The district offices, which are really most forward-facing, they're all across the boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: They're the ones that are looking at the battery cabinet siding.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay, so separate teams and eight-week timeline.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You believe you have the staff to maintain a two-month turnaround to approve applications moving forward?

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Yes, we do the best we can with the workload.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: And they also do not only permits but a special event, so particular times of the year, such as the holiday time, summertime, things like that.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Their workload increases even more.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I want to just...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank especially my colleagues, Council Members Wong and Felice, for letting me cut the line.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And thank you for the thoughtful, these responses were very helpful.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We'd love to follow up and just get some more information in writing.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Ariola pauses and calls Schulman on Zoom. Schulman says education is not enough and enforcement is needed, notes delivery workers are dying, and asks why FDNY still has issues with Councilmember Wong's bill given LA County restrictions on batteries in living spaces. Currao asks for clarification and says the LA restrictions may apply to energy storage systems, not micromobility devices.
chapters.title: Schulman urges enforcement and asks about LA County battery restrictions

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you for indulging me.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We're going to go to Zoom right now with Council Member Shulman for a statement and a few questions.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you to both chairs.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: You know, I really feel this is a very important subject.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And I also want to say that, Commissioner, you know, it's great that we're doing education and public service announcements and all of that.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: But we have to, you know, that's not going to cut it.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We need to really do a lot of enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We need to not do the status quo.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The department has concerns about a bunch of the legislation, but, you know, we got to do something new here because the people, and by the way, you know, you talk about not wanting to impede or

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: harm the delivery Easter's and all of that, but they're the ones that are dying in these fires.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: You know, we had the speaker has been a real leader and.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Abiding the status quo, which you saw when we

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We passed the horse carriage bill recently, ending the horse carriage industry.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So, and there were unintended consequences of that as well.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So we really have to take a deep dive here because, I mean, there was one person that died there, but there were six people that died in Councilmember Zhuang's district.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So one of the questions I have is that I was doing some research and I saw in LA County.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: You can't have batteries as restricted to detached garages and structures, and they're not allowed in apartment buildings unless there's permission given by the fire department.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I want to know why you still have an issue with Councilmember Wong's bill.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Councilwoman, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I ask for some clarification?

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: You said about another jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: L.A., L.A.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: County.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: L.A.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: County, you said attachment to the garage.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Are you talking about an energy store?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: They're generally restricted.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: They're prohibited installing batteries inside habitable living spaces, closets or basements unless granted a specific.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Approval by the fire department.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Is that for micromobility devices or energy storage systems such as a Tesla Powerwall?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Batteries.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The ion batteries.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: So I guess also to answer it by taking two things.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: So currently right now, you cannot put in a small energy storage system within a living.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: It's not an energy source in the e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The e-bikes are banned from.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Apartments or anything else, they have to be kept outside.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: They have to be kept in a separate storage area.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So that's what I'm asking you, because I think that Councilmember Wong's bill is very appropriate here.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We have to stop people from dying in these fires.

chapters.summary: Currao agrees with a whole-community approach, says FDNY wants to lean into outdoor charging and collaborate with building owners, and notes LA is a different urban environment. Schulman ends her questions.
chapters.title: Currao discusses outdoor charging and comparing jurisdictions

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Completely agree.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: I think it's going to take really a whole community approach because, as has been said before, we want people to be safe.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: We want to lean into outside charging.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: That also requires collaboration with building owners to be able to offer other types of outdoor storage that is secure, that is fire safe, that can really address our concerns for fire safety, outdoor storage,

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: as well as if that's, say, a micro mobility device or e-bike that someone depends on for their living,

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: that it is also secure and it is something that they can access and then use for their daily work or activities.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So my question is, have you looked at other jurisdictions and what they do in these situations?

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Yeah, so I think certainly we can continually interact with other jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: In fact, two days ago, we just held a regional cold conference, so we had multiple jurisdictions right in fire department headquarters talking about situations such as these.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: And I think also we have to consider that L.A.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Is a different, in some ways, a different urban environment, right?

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: It's such a dense urban landscape, right?

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: So we have to always apply our code revisions, our different policies within the reality of what we're facing in obviously a dense urban environment.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That was, that's the extent of my question.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Areola.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And thank you, Chair Sanchez, for your questions as well.

chapters.summary: Ariola moves to Feliz. Feliz thanks FDNY, says the city is not doing everything within its power, and asks what else can be done at point of sale to stop defective batteries. Flynn says point-of-sale inspections ensure untested batteries are not sold, but many uncertified batteries were sold before Local Law 39 and are now aging out.
chapters.title: Feliz frames battery fire crisis and asks what else can be done at point of sale

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We'll now go to Councilmember Felice and then Wong.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I just want to start by, again, thanking all of you for all the work that you do on this important issue of fire safety.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Every single day, well, almost every single day, we see the videos.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Firefighters risking their own lives to save people in our city.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And our city is incredibly grateful.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And thankful for those sacrifices.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So I just want to start with the line that Councilmember Shulman mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We have to stop people from dying in these fires.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: The federal government has to act, and I know there's been a lot of proposals at the federal level,

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: The federal government needs to act.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: These are many defective batteries that are obviously entering from other parts of the world.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But the impression that I'm getting from this, and I've been working on this issue for three, four, maybe five years now.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You know, we passed my UL certification bill, also the bill that requires that the companies provide safe and certified e-bikes to workers who don't have one.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: The impression that I'm getting is that, and again, the federal government hashtag, but the impression that I'm getting is that we as a city are not doing everything within our power, including our power to regulate.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We are not doing everything within our power to put an end to this crisis.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: This is a horrible crisis.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: There's over 400 fires this year.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: More than we've ever had.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And one thing that I don't want is that next year, a year from today, we have another oversight hearing and the numbers have only escalated more than they've already had.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So a few questions.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: As we know, e-bikes are a top cause of fires.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Again, over 400 fires this year already, more fires than we've ever had.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: This is a real crisis.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: This is obviously a crisis that exists due to many issues, many complicated issues.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: One thing that I'm always asking myself is how much of it is due to, let's say, education.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Education is obviously something that we should always promote, good on every issue.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: It resolves issues.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But I've spoken with a lot of individuals who use these e-bikes, and the impression that I get is that the problem is much, much more deeper than just education.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Many of them say,

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: They have a battery that is not certified.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: They know that uncertified batteries can cause safety issues, and they're also concerned about that, the fact that they're using a body that's not certified.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But they say, let's say, they say the delivery worker, they need batteries that can last a very long time, and obviously the batteries that are not certified, they last much longer without needing to be recharged versus the UL certified ones, which you'll have to recharge much more often.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And obviously they're in the streets 10, 15 hours a day, so they obviously don't have the resources to...

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Be able to have access to that or be able to use that safe battery and be able to do their job without obstacles, including related to charging.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So when I have conversations like that, it just seems like the problem is much deeper than education.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We can educate, but many of them already know and they still use it due to those infrastructure issues.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Related issues.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'm always wondering how much of it is due to education, but also how much of it is due to lack of access to the safe and certified e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We again passed a bill requiring that the companies help and so much more.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And also how much of it is due to other problems that we are not tackling or we're not even discussing.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And again, a super complicated issue.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But I think one thing that we could all agree on is that these batteries are incredibly dangerous.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: They pose serious public safety threats for all of us, not only those that are using it, but also for entire communities, including the neighbors where these batteries are being stored.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So a few questions.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: One of the point of sale.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Another one on the legislation that I passed requiring that delivery companies provide safe and certified e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: On the point of sale, so earlier you mentioned that we have to tackle the issue from a point of sale.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You also mentioned that, or the impression that I got was that the FDNY has practically done everything within your power to enforce the point of sale rules.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You've enforced and you've inspected and re-inspected, you visited.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Every possible, every store that sells e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So what else can be done at the point of sale to stop these defective e-bike batteries from entering our streets?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And thank you for your partnership on this on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: You've been a real supporter of this throughout and some of this we couldn't have done without you.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And as I mentioned earlier, your local law 39 is is very, very similar to Congressmember Torres's bill that he proposed.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And with the support of Senator Jill Brand and Schumer, thankfully, that that was passed last night.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And I think that will have a lasting effect on these devices to encourage high quality devices to be imported and sold and manufactured here in this country.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we won't see these these bad batteries coming into into the country.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: What, as I mentioned earlier, we do we do education as well when we do these point of sale inspections.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We inspect for violations of law, but we also inspect for violations of the code as well.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We're not just there doing a lithium ion inspection.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: It's an inspection of all aspects of the store because a battery can be perfect, but subjected to fire, that battery will fail.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What else, though, can be done at the point of sale to stop these defective e-bike batteries from entering our streets?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Well, the point-of-sale inspection ensures that the untested batteries are not sold.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And if we discover that, we will violate them for that.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But it seems like you've done everything within your power as the regulations currently allow.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And by the way, not blaming you, obviously, we're the ones passing legislation and all of you are the ones doing the enforcing.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But it seems like you've done everything within your power to fully enforce that rule and the numbers have only escalated.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, unfortunately, there are a great number of batteries that are out on our streets that are not certified and were sold prior to the enacting of your legislation.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So they're still out there, and I think most of those devices, I think, are kind of nearing their end of life.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: They've been beat up at this point.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And a lot of these fires we're seeing now this year, we're seeing in the back of sanitation trucks also.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So there's a huge issue with the disposal of these as well.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: People should visit the DSNY website to learn how to properly dispose of these, learn where the drop-off points are that they can go and be safe in the disposal.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: of these fires this year were in the back of sanitation trucks.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks what percentage of e-bikes are certified versus uncertified and how defective batteries enter communities. Flynn says it is impossible to determine after sale, estimates less than half are uncertified, and says some bad actors sell secondhand or on the street. Feliz argues the city lacks a grip on the root problem.
chapters.title: Feliz asks what percentage of e-bikes are uncertified and how they enter streets

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So if you were to guess, I don't know if there's any studies done on this issue, but if you were to guess,

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: out of all the e-bike batteries or e-bikes that are in our streets being used for commercial and personal purposes, what percentage would you say are certified e-bikes versus uncertified?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: That's very, it's extremely difficult for us to determine.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: If you were to guess, though, based on everything that you see in our streets and all the investigations, would you say at least half of them are uncertified?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, once it leaves the store, I feel it's impossible to determine whether that battery is certified or not.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Based on the information that you've learned on this issue, and all of you have done a lot of work on this issue,

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: How are these batteries entering our streets?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: To me, it seems pretty clear they're not entering from storefront businesses.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: It seems like there's a black market that's allowing them to just inundate our communities.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We have seen some bad actors there, people trying to subvert the law.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We can only act on the things that we're aware of.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So there has been some bad actors that are selling these things on the ground or selling them secondhand.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Some of these fires, we learned they were purchased for somebody on the street.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So they don't know the nexus of this battery.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: The fire we had in the Bronx a couple weeks ago, that was purchased from a friend.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So we have no idea where it was purchased or whether that was a certified device or not.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Do you have any information on that, though?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Is that the crux of the problem?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Defective e-bikes or uncertified e-bikes entering our streets through the black market versus storefronts.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: The impression that I'm getting is that, again, all of you have done everything as allowed per regulations and laws, but it seems like we're not tackling the root of the problem because if they're entering through the black market, you can enforce

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: every single day visit, every single e-bike sale company, every single day, but if that's not where the defective e-bikes are coming from, then...

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: we're not tackling the problem from the root.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, I think a lot of these devices I mentioned were out on our streets prior to enacting this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So it's very hard to determine where they were purchased and whether they were certified or not.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And as the commissioner mentioned, I think a lot of the people that utilize these devices, they don't know.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: They think they purchased a legitimate device.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: They went to the store.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We had a fatal in Queens a couple years ago where the device was purchased at the Queens Mall.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: If I purchase a device at the Queens Center Mall, I think I'm purchasing a quality device.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: People are under the assumption that these are quality products and not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We've engaged with the online retailers as well.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: With the help of DCWP, we've reached out to Amazon, to Walmart, all those retailers that would sell these products in the city to make them aware of your bill that they need to comply with the local law here.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: They've been pretty good partners in that.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Based on the fact, though, we...

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: passed the bill, when was it, about two, three years ago.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: It took effect maybe like two years ago.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Based on the fact that two years ago, the law took effect that prohibits individuals from selling non-UAL certified e-bike batteries.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And I don't have any data on this, but the impression I'm getting is that at least half of the e-bikes out there are not certified e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Isn't it reasonable to conclude that these storefront businesses are not the problem anymore, but instead the black market, Craigslist, maybe even, I don't know, whatever illegitimate business that's not like an official one with a storefront?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We have a great relationship with the Delaristas as well.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: We've met with them several times.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I talk to them whenever I get a chance as to where they're purchasing these bikes or who's selling these products to them.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And I think, again, they've been doing this for a while.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: The delivery industry boomed during COVID.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: People weren't leaving their house.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: There was a demand for that fast delivery.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: The restaurants were closed.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: There wasn't an option for them.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: So I think that the boom now, we're starting to see those devices fail.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: They've been subjected to the elements here.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But I guess my question is.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Would you say that the sales through the black market, would you say that is the problem on the issue of the new uncertified e-bikes that are not in our communities, that are entering our streets?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I think the sales currently, where we stand today, I think the sales on the black market are very...

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I think we're seeing high-quality products that are sold, new products that are sold here in the city are high-quality products that do comply with the law.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Then how is it that we have so many uncertified e-bikes in our communities?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So you're saying that, number one, the black market is not the problem, and number two, we have laws that require that batteries be UL certified and that you've done everything you possibly could by inspecting and re-inspecting.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So then how are these batteries entering our communities?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I mean, the impression that I'm getting, again, is that at least half of the e-bikes out there are not certified.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: They're coming from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, I wouldn't, if just anecdotally, I would not put that high of a number on it.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I think it's a little bit less than that.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: And I would support that buyback program.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I think it's a fantastic idea.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: Having the apps be more engaged, treating their, I see them as employees of the app.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: The apps sometimes see them as contractors.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: I think they have a responsibility to make sure that they're

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: employees are safe.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Flynn
utterances.text: They need to provide them with materials to educate them and support them in having safe products.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Right, yes.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And, you know, obviously I'm not an expert on the issue of you all certified versus not certified, but I've done a lot of research to be able to quickly tell or be able to somewhat distinguish the certified ones versus the uncertified ones.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I represent the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I spend a lot of time in my district.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'm usually

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: taking a hard look at e-bikes when I see them because obviously e-bike fires is a big problem in the Bronx and based on what I see generally these are the these the e-bikes that I see are from brands that are known to be

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: not certified so I think the big question that we need to figure out and that requires a lot of attention is

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: How are these batteries and how are these defective e-bikes entering our communities?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: It seems like we don't have, as a city, we don't have a good grip of that question.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Again, if you're saying that you've inspected and re-inspected and issued fines and visited every single e-bike sale company in the city that has a storefront and also...

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: The black market sales is not a problem, then we have to figure out, I mean, they have to be answering somehow.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And that is the question that I think we don't have a good understanding of.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And I think resolution of this fire safety crisis is going to require us to give that issue a lot of attention.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And again, I'll just reiterate, we've done a lot.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Obviously, this is not an issue.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: This is a complicated issue that requires many different phases.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You know, we passed the UL certification law, also the trade-in program.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But if you trade in one defective e-bike for a safe one, and while you get that one defective e-bike off the streets and 100 new ones uncertified onto the streets, we are never, ever going to resolve this issue.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So it just seems like we as a city are not doing everything within our power to regulate to truly, but truly resolve this very important fire safety crisis.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And that explains why the numbers have only escalated.

chapters.summary: Currao says the federal legislation passed last night is important because online purchases can bypass local standards. Bonsignore says FDNY must keep pressure on point of sale and continue enforcement while working with the Council on solutions.
chapters.title: Currao and Bonsignore cite federal legislation and point-of-sale pressure

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Councilman, if I could add, I think there's a third leg to this.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: That's why the federal legislation passed last evening is so important, right?

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: Because with a couple of clicks on your computer, right, you can get devices, right, that even if you started out with certified and now you say, hey, I'm just, you know, I want a cheaper product,

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: that battery management system, that charging system is not designed like that.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: And now, you know, through the mail, they deliver it to you, and, you know, you're getting something that's on, you know, a legitimate website, but it's still unsafe.

utterances.speaker: Thomas Currao
utterances.text: So I think that's where that federal legislation is going to be really important.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: It's also very important that we continue to keep the pressure on the point of sale, though, right?

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Because we want them to be uncomfortable getting any product or anything from a lesser, you know, certified kind of, you know, stock, right?

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We want them to know that we're watching.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We want them to know we're going to show up.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And that's what we continue to do.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So as we continue to navigate and try to, you know, find every direction that we can go in as far as the incoming stock into the city, we still have to continue doing the things that we're doing.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And I think the fire department, you know, has been ringing the bell since 2021.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: I think, you know, it was the fire department that identified this and started this entire conversation across the country.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And now, you know, we're seeing that the federal government now got something.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: thing that is going to be helpful for us, that they're going to set standards, and we can continue to work within our cities.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: And the fire department is happy to work with all of you to come up with solutions and things that make sense that we can actually accomplish together.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: To keep people safe because we don't want to see these fires either.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Right, of course.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: Every fire that we have, I'm putting first responders and firefighters in danger.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: You know, every fire that we have, family members are losing loved ones.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: We want to make sure that we're coming up with good solutions.

utterances.speaker: Lillian Bonsignore
utterances.text: So we look forward to continuing our work.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Yes, and likewise.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And thank you so much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And again, I think my overall point, though, is that we have to tackle the issue from a point of sale, but we also have to understand the limitations.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Again, the impression that I'm getting is that you've done everything you possibly could to...

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Strictly enforce the rules, but they're not grabbing the problem from its root.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: There's obviously limitations that we face, right, when products are being sold through Craigslist.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Amazon, very difficult to enforce.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So I guess the overall point is that it seems like based on the point of sale rules and the powers that you currently have, you've done everything you possibly could, and it's nowhere near enough given that, you know, the fires have only escalated.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So it seems like the overall point here is that it seems like we have to think about other creative ways of tackling this problem so that we as a city could be able to say, hey,

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: there are still some issues, but we have done everything we possibly could on this issue, and I think right now we are not able to say that.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
