utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I really appreciate the extra time.

chapters.summary: Esposito says he contacted LA County Fire Department leadership and the restrictions Schulman mentioned apply to battery energy storage systems, not e-bike batteries in residential units.
chapters.title: Chief Esposito clarifies LA County restrictions apply to energy storage

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Chair, I just have a clarification.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So this morning I've been in touch with the leadership of the Los Angeles County Fire Department, and those restrictions apply that Councilmember Shulman was talking about, apply to battery energy storage systems.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: They do not have a restriction on e-bike batteries in residential units.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, thank you for that clarification.

chapters.summary: Wong says his office refers complaints about indoor battery charging to FDNY but gets little follow-up. An FDNY representative says since 2022 they have received over 900 complaints, respond within 12 hours, and have a 95% clear rate, but will follow up on caller feedback.
chapters.title: Wong asks what happens when residents report dangerous battery charging

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Councilmember Wong.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I have some questions regarding what exactly happens when residents report dangerous battery charges.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My office regularly receives complaints about lithium-ion batteries and mobility devices being charged inside apartments, homes, and on private property.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We refer these concerns to FDNY, but too often we receive little follow-up or explanation about what happened after the notification.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So my question is, when FDNY receives one of these complaints, what exactly happens?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Who investigates and what determines whether an inspection takes place?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Councilman, thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So since 2022, we've received over 900 different complaints,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: some through 311, some directly through our customer service center, as well as urgent issues that can come to our fire department operations center.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They can be handled a couple of ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If it's extremely urgent, it's something that our fire units will go out right away to check out, and they can also bring in our special inspection unit,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: our inspectors any time of day to follow up in terms of needing any advice for enforcement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But within 12 hours, we are dedicated to go out to check out that situation, to issue a violation order, which requires a re-inspection or an FDI summons or a criminal summons, depending on what's done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So a lot of times we do it in conjunction with other agencies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And, you know, so we've handled, you know, over like a 95% clear rate.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So the caller, how does that person know that whether the dangerous condition was addressed?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: How do I know anything was done?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: To the initial, right, right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I would have to, to be honest with you, I think I'd have to follow up on that in terms of like our feedback to the caller.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I believe our customer service center does send a reply back to the originator of the complaint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But I could get you, you know, sir, I can get you numbers on that and follow up with that.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You can send it to.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, my follow-up is what if the FDNY cannot access the private property?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Nobody's home.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: They refuse to open the door.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What happens?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Well, there's only really two ways that we can actually get to access.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So one is obviously that the person in there gives us access, or exigent circumstances if we have something showing that looks like it's dangerous, smoke, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But if there is no access to that, we'll have to come back to that particular location and do a follow-up inspection.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And next day or after a certain number of days, because I don't see that being written anywhere.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Like, what's your process to investigate further?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I think that's my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it depends on the nature of the particular call, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we certainly, like I said, we have over a 90% closure rate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we're definitely getting back there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They're very, very diligent, the team that we have, the special inspection unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In fact, they're actually actively today doing a seal on a particular business that is operating illegally, and they're going to do one tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So they're very, very active.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But as far as getting data for getting back to the original caller, I'll certainly get that back to the committee.

chapters.summary: Wong says many cases seem closed because FDNY cannot access property or reach anyone. The FDNY representative says the data does not support that, citing 471 inspections and 255 summonses.
chapters.title: Wong asks about access issues and closure rates for complaints

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Because it seemed to me that a lot of these cases were closed because you don't have access to the property or you couldn't get a hold of anyone.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: to respond to your inquiry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So the data doesn't support that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I mean, we had over 471 inspections, 255 summonses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We were out there a lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I think our data supports a different conclusion.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

chapters.summary: Wong asks if FDNY supports removing the residential charging exception. FDNY says it wants balance because many people have no other place to store or charge devices, and as written the bill may not be enforceable. They discuss needing outdoor storage options that meet safety standards.
chapters.title: Wong asks whether FDNY supports Intro 920 and how it would be enforced

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: All right, my...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I have one question.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I hope I can squeeze two questions.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: It seemed to me, based on the testimony of the commissioner, that my bill 920 is...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is something that you may not support because it says the department is working within the administration and the council to achieve the right balance to optimize safety for everyone.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Can I hear from you, like, does the FDNY support Intro 920 to removing the residential charging exception?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, we did say we're happy to try to work with you to achieve the right balance because there is no other option for people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we're concerned about how that would be.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: There's no space to store the bikes outside?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is that the concern?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There's no other option for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So many people live in buildings and many people don't have options to put it someplace else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we want to make sure that we're being mindful of the people's reality and the reality of what we need to happen, which is to store and charge these things outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So as written, you know, we would like to see something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That is striking a better balance, and we'd be happy to work with you to try to come up with that language.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So, in other words, we need to create spaces for them to store their bikes.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We certainly need to provide options.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Like racks, right?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Or bike racks outside?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We need to provide some kind of legitimate options that meet the standards of charging and storing these lithium-ion batteries.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: But would bike racks be a legitimate option?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Like racks alone?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Only if you don't have a battery on them.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So what about like...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: and hold boxes outside the apartment buildings where they can literally store like a mailbox.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that technology is the technology that is currently the subject of many conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It just doesn't exist yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So again, I would love to sit with you and figure out what would actually work so that we can keep people safe.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I'll save my questions for round two.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: If you wouldn't mind, you can finish, because I don't think we're going to go to a round two, because it's only just us.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Would this intro 920 be enforceable?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Let me ask you this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I don't know how it would be enforced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we have real concerns about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I mean, if the way it's written, I don't think we have the capabilities ourselves to enforce such a law.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: See, okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Now, again, the spirit of this is to get people to stop storing batteries in their houses, stop storing bikes.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We know, we know, I talked to delivery men, they may have more than one battery in the house, they may have three or four because they work every day.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So we do not want that to happen and we want to provide, to make the building safe, we want them to stop storing these.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Batteries in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We are with you in that spirit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We just have to find the right language that works for people and is enforceable.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So would you agree that if we ask that these apartment building owners put bike racks outside or put up storage boxes for the batteries to be stored, is that something that you would support?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Only if they are able to meet the standard that we're looking for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So that it wouldn't just be a normal bike box or, you know, a rack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It would have to be able to contain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: a fire that could happen as a result of that battery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I think we are on the same path together, but we have to really take a good look at the technology's capabilities in order for it to actually be safe.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: FDNY says battery cabinets are the intended solution, developed with industry and interagency partners, and they expect continued roundtables on new technologies and battery chemistries.
chapters.title: FDNY explains battery cabinets as safe outdoor storage option

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Can you turn on the mic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sorry, my mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's what the battery cabinets are for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's why we worked so closely with the industry as well as other interagency partners to have that option out there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Because that addresses your concern, addresses what the commissioner is saying in terms of safe storage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We had a working group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: A couple of years ago, we came out with multiple recommendations collaboratively with the manufacturers of cabinets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I expect that that will continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I believe that we have some roundtables coming up as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that's important because they're looking at new technologies too, right, and how we can make this more accessible, more safe, different types of technology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So it's still an ongoing conversation as well as the battery technologies that are out there, the different battery chemistries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There are other ones that are more stable.

chapters.summary: Wong notes 18 electrical fire fatalities and asks what extension cord or power strip is safe for e-bikes. FDNY recommends limiting extension cords and power strips and plugging e-bike batteries directly into the wall.
chapters.title: Wong asks about extension cords and power strips for e-bike charging

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, one last question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, in the Commissioner's report, you have 18 fatalities occur during fires that were related to electrical issues.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: including electrical wiring and power strips.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Now, to the layperson, he may not know which extension cord or power strip is appropriate for the e-bike that he just bought.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And my question is, what's the standard here?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What is the minimal...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Extension cord or power strip you need to buy and is there something we can do to to educate the public like

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: our recommendation is that you limit the use of extension cords and power strips especially if you are going to plug in an appliance plug in a

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: e-bike battery that should be plugged directly into the wall and not use any extension cord or any power strip.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, so whatever cable that comes with the bike, that should go directly into the wall outlet.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: No extension cords.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I think that outreach is important.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks Wong and calls Sanchez. Sanchez asks if the city can require sellers to notify buyers of unlawful products or provide no-cost remedies. FDNY says DCWP could not attend and they do not have that answer, but notes DCWP has issued 86 cease-and-desist letters to online sellers, 41 summonses, and 26 businesses came into compliance.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks whether city can require sellers to notify buyers of unlawful products

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Chair Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Areola, and thank you for the endurance of answering all of our colleagues'questions.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: This is such an important topic.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So I just have two more sets of questions.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: First, this might be for DCWP, so let us know if it is, and you can defer and we can have the discussion later.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But does the city have the ability to require sellers to notify buyers of any unlawful products that they may have erroneously sold?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Can the city require sellers to provide no-cost remedies for products sold unlawfully?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Please excuse my pause, but they were unable to come today, so they sent some answers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm just looking for the question that you asked them so I can give you the appropriate answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So would you just repeat that question for me?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Yeah, essentially, can the city force sellers?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: To do more for buyers who have purchased unlawful products.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So if a product does not comply with city regulations or...

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: But if it is not on the list of answers that you have, we can always follow up with GCWP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I could follow up if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I will just say that there is no obligation on the establishment to notify the...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: No, not currently.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So we should explore that authority.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Does the city have the authority to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I have something that seems a little bit pertinent, so I can just.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It has to do with how many online retailers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I don't know if you're interested in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So it's how many online retailers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Have DCWP pursued enforcement against for failing to comply with product safety requirements?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Is that important to you?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It is, in the case of online sellers, we have issued at least 86 cease and desist letters to identified companies selling these products.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: 26 businesses have come into compliance with following these summonses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We've issued at least 41 summonses to online sellers that did not comply with our cease and desist letters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we actively work with these businesses to move them into compliance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: ongoing investigations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So it seems like they do have some kind of interaction there to try to address the sellers.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Yeah, and thank you Commissioner for being a team player and answering on their behalf because that doesn't always happen so I really do appreciate it.

chapters.summary: Sanchez raises concerns about construction next to homes, smaller sites under seven stories, and the 1321 Flatbush tragedy. DOB says New Yorkers should call 311 for structural concerns, describes Chapter 33 as rigorous, and says the 1321 investigation is ongoing with a third-party engineering firm.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks DOB about construction safety and 1321 Flatbush collapse

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, so here's my last question and it's a bit off topic because today's hearing of course is on residential fires but this is for buildings.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I started to ask it, this is the third hearing of the Housing and Buildings Committee this week, but I did start to ask it earlier this week at a different hearing, so I wanted to follow up with our first deputy commissioner and our DOB leadership.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So while today's hearing focuses on residential fires, the larger issue is how we keep New Yorkers safe within their homes and how we prevent tragedies, of course, before they happen.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: One of the complaints that we hear often as council members is from homeowners, many seniors, who are worried about construction happening right next door to them.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And I want to highlight Councilmember Wong, who asked about this very issue at a previous hearing.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: These seniors and these constituents are concerned about cracks appearing in their walls, damage to their foundations, and understandably fear for the structural integrity of their homes.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: At the October 21st construction safety hearing of the Housing Committee, we raised concerns about the lower level of scrutiny that the Department of Buildings applies to smaller construction sites, including statutory gaps that limit the oversight.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: For example, the fact that DOB is not required under current law

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: to review site safety training cards and logs at certain smaller sites, those under seven stories.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So, in light of the horrific tragedy at 1321 in Flatbush, these concerns have become more urgent.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The question is, what is the Department of Buildings doing to ensure that construction on one property does not put a neighboring home and family at risk?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What inspections and safeguards are required, particularly at smaller construction sites?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And what happens when homeowners report cracks or other signs of structural damage?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Gothamist reported that the Department of Buildings approved construction plans that did not include shoring or underpinning to protect the neighboring building at the 1321 site.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So why were those plans approved without those protections?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'll take those questions just one at a time if I could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: First and foremost, I think if any New Yorker has a concern, a structural stability concern with their building, I would encourage all New Yorkers to call 311.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Especially if it's related to shaking or vibrating of their building, I would highly encourage all New Yorkers to call 311.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Our response time for those A complaints, those shaking and vibrating complaints, is just over three hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I would encourage all New Yorkers, as I said, to call 311 if they do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: See cracks of their buildings or if they feel any type of vibration or shaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: With regards to the requirements for protection of adjoining properties,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: our Chapter 33 requirements for construction safety are, I would say, the most rigorous in the country, if not the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For instance, and I didn't just print this out for today, this is my copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: This is 167 pages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That is the length and breadth of our chapter 33.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: safeguards during construction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I happened to do just a little bit of research beforehand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The International Building Codes Chapter 33 requirements are seven pages long, and I looked at a few other jurisdictions nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Those are respectively still single digits in the number of pages with regards to construction safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So our section in the New York City Building Code for simply just the protection of adjoining properties is longer than entire jurisdictions construction safety requirements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: All that being said, we are always looking to strengthen our laws and strengthen our regulations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Specifically when it comes to the protection of all New Yorkers in buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Every day people come into buildings and are in buildings every single day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And like I said, if they have a concern, please call 311.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Not sure if I answered all your questions, but I think I got most of them.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And I agree that we have in-depth construction codes that are many, many times longer and more detailed than other jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But I suppose just to close this one out, I was hoping that you could...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Directly address Gotham's concern that underpinning was insufficient at this site and where we are with the investigation and what the timeline could be for 1321.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: With regards to the investigation, our investigation is ongoing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We are working closely with our partners in law enforcement to implement that investigation, but it is ongoing, so unfortunately I cannot discuss it at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: However, the New York City Department of Buildings is engaging with a third-party engineering firm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We sent out an emergency procurement contract the day after this incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we are bringing on a third-party consulting firm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: To do that investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: With regards to the specifics of the supportive excavation along exposure four of that construction site,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: that wasn't underpinning that was shown on the supportive excavation drawings, but rather a benching detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that benching detail, as you mentioned, went through a full plan examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Earlier in the year, in 2025, we eliminated through a building bulletin all self-cert applications for underpinning and supportive excavation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So that was about a year and a half ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So all those types of plan examination are fully reviewed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And with specific...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: to the benching as I as you mentioned on exposure for 1321 Flatbush Avenue

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: when developing any plans whether those are supportive excavation or structural any plans that are submitted to the Department of Buildings it is the registered design professional that is signing and sealing those plans to make sure

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: that those plans meet all the building code requirements, but not only that, to make sure it meets all the site-specific requirements with regards to those specific sites.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And again, it is their role very specifically and their requirement as a registered design professional, as a PERRA,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: to make sure that that work is being done on those drawings safely and per the code.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that is the role of the design professional.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: With regards to the benching detail very specifically, that is a detail that is industry practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That similar type of excavation design has been safely performed here in New York City for decades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We are, again, as I said, we're reviewing everything as part of the investigation, and we will make that investigation by the third-party engineer that we're retaining public, as we always do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, First Deputy Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And is there a timeline for the results of that investigation or the third party's report to the agency?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's ongoing, and we'll keep you abreast on that.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I will ensure to keep knocking on your door.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much to all of you and Chair Areola.

chapters.summary: Ariola notes Councilmember Rita Joseph has joined. Joseph thanks FDNY and asks what DOB and FDNY do proactively to prevent lithium-ion battery fires in multifamily buildings and how the city strengthens outreach, inspection, and enforcement. FDNY describes educational materials for building owners, website translations, and a multilingual call center.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about proactive measures and multilingual outreach

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We've been joined by Councilmember Rita Joseph, and she does have a question.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: On behalf of the neighboring district over in District 40, we want to say thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you for being on hand.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you for serving our communities in time of need.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So on behalf of District 40, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: My question is, what are the proactive measures are the Department of Buildings and FDMY take to prevent residential fires caused by lithium-ion batteries,

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: particularly in multifamily buildings, and how can the city strengthen outreach, inspection, and enforcement to ensure residents are equipped with knowledge, resources to safely charge, store, and dispose of these batteries?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: If it was asked already, I forgive me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We covered some of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think a lot of, and I really appreciate your support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It means a lot to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And it means a lot to us to have the support of the community as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have a robust education campaign.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have educational materials that we give to building owners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They're required to give those materials to people that come and sign leases to educate them on not only the dangers of lithium-ion batteries, but our other fire safety concerns.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Are these available in different languages or?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We distributed to the building owners and then they distributed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We don't know who we're targeting at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We do have our website is available in different languages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So if you want to go to FTMYsmart.org and you can see our safety messaging.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That will be in different languages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So our call center, I believe now, we're developing different languages for our BFP call center as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We've made a lot of innovation there with the AI agent that is able to serve the concerns of the community also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So that's a huge success for us in Bureau of Fire Prevention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We go out, as the Commissioner mentioned earlier, we're out at schools and conducting engagement with the community every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We estimate that we've...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We've been able to communicate with over half a million people just this year alone with fire safety messaging.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And lithium ion is definitely at the forefront of our fire safety message.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks about partnering with clergy, faith-based organizations, senior centers, and doctor's offices. FDNY says it partners with community leaders, faith-based organizations, schools, senior centers, and NYCHA, and has reached about half a million people in person plus social media and PSAs.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about partnerships with older adults and faith-based groups

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Are we thinking of older adults maybe partnering with clergy as well, faith-based as well, because a lot of our community members are in churches, are in schools, are in doctor's offices as well?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, we partner with everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So the community leaders, the faith-based organizations, the schools,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: senior centers, NYCHA, you know, anybody who wants to work with us, you know, we push ourselves on them because this information is just so important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we have done about a half a million folks outreach in person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But we've also gotten lots of interaction online.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We've done social media campaigns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We've done PSAs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're about to embark on a five-week campaign that is across different types of medias, ethnic media, radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we're getting the message out as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We do have materials in multiple languages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We also have recently developed an app that is transational.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: My brain is starting to shut down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So it can be conversational, trans.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So in real time, we can talk back and forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It will cover about 28 different languages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we are doing everything in our power to reach as many people as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I'll just plug here because I plugged this and you gave me a great opportunity to do it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm asking everybody to engage in like Fire Safety Friday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Where every single one of us put things on our own personal and professional social media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If you go to fdmy smart.org, we have lots of tips and information there that you could share about fire safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think if we all do that at the same time every day, you know, once a week on Fridays,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: more people will be introduced to some of the life-saving information that we have to offer them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I would certainly appreciate your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Oh, definitely.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And don't forget the WhatsApp group chats.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: They're also very active with community members.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks what investments strengthen fire safety infrastructure, tenant education, and evacuation plans in older buildings. FDNY cites annual fire safety bulletins, fire safety guides, posted notices, and translations into 13 languages.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about fire safety infrastructure and evacuation planning

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And also concerning inspections.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Throughout the city, our fire companies are out in the communities every day doing building inspection to inspect the common areas of the building

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: for fire safe and fire code compliance.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: My next question is beyond responding to fires after they occur, and I said, what additional investments or initiatives are being implemented to strengthen?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: and fire safety infrastructure in residential buildings, educate tenants, building owners of fire prevention, and ensure residents have clear evacuation plans and access to functioning

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: fire safety systems, particularly in older buildings and vulnerable communities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So that, thank you very much for the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's baked into our code and our regulations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So one of the things that's very helpful, and we just produced another one, is our annual fire safety bulletin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It covers lithium ion, but it also covers a breadth of the, you know, the most common issues that we find, whether it's electrical or lithium ion or unsafe storage, any of those type of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We also have fire safety guides, and this is a great partnership with building owners, building managers to make sure that that is getting to the residents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In addition, fire safety notices that are required to be posted on the doors, and that's really important because it tells you, you know, are you in this type of building?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's a combustible building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Are you in a building that's more like fireproof?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And then different decision-making points in a fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know, we find that, you know, sheltering in one situation versus immediate evacuation in the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So that is something that we invest a lot of effort into.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And as the first deputy commissioner and commissioner said before, translating to 13 different languages.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how FDNY partners with CUNY and expands career pipelines. FDNY describes working with PAL, the FDNY High School EMT program, youth organizations, colleges, driver's license support, and veteran services to recruit into EMS and fire service.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about FDNY and CUNY workforce pipeline

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: It's also important if I didn't do the workforce pipeline as the higher education chair, how is FDNY partnering with CUNY to recruit engaged college students who are interested in pursuing a career in firefighters, emergency service?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What opportunities exist now to expand these partnerships through career pipeline, internship, mentorship, workforce development programs that encourage more young New Yorkers to pursue a career in your field?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I know we have the FDNY High School.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Just want to know what's the pipeline once they finish with FDNY High School.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What's the handover to CUNY?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a great question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we're working within our communities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're working very closely with PAL to try to develop these partnerships, which we've been quite successful at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They are being newly integrated in these different areas outside of our high school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In our high school, I'll just tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We've changed some of their curriculum so that in their junior and senior year of high school, we have them for four years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So in their junior and senior year of high school, they do a two-year-long EMT program.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They start in their junior year, and they end in their senior year, and they can graduate being a New York State certified EMT.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Which allows for them to get into the civil service arena and apply for the job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we will help them do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: On the outside of the high school, we're building pipelines through all the

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: the youth organizations, including the colleges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Some of them are paying for their driver's license instruction because they need that in order to get hired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're giving them, you know, we're working out different partnerships so that the EMT certification is something that they can leave that pipeline with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And the reason I talk about EMT certification is that that is a quick.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Like introduction into the civil service environment within the fire department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we're excited about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know, the other partnership that we are building right now is with the veteran services.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The commissioner and I,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: have met and talked about pipelining people who are coming out of the military into the fire department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Because it's such a familiar environment, you know, you're coming out of one ranked structured environment into another, and they are very good with adrenaline, like us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So yeah, we're talking with everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We really want

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: the youth in our city to understand what an incredibly wonderful job this is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I mean, I know we talk about very difficult things when we come here, and we look to problem solve with the council, and that is certainly something we look forward to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But the reality of our world is we absolutely love what we do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know, we love doing the work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We love taking care of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It is...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: heartbreaking sometimes, but it is no longer, or maybe never has been what we do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's just who we are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I think the kids, some of the youth out there have this in them and they just don't know it yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we're excited to go out and share this opportunity with them and guide them into the department so they can have

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: incredible careers like many of us have had.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Wonderful.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I would love to be a partner in that space and working on that workforce development space.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I came from education before I was a council member, so this is important work in advancing our city and making sure our young people know that their career is opportunities here.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So thank you so much, chairs.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I would also ask that you just share then join FDNY on your socials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Join FDNY is all of our recruitment information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Whoever's your media, social media person, send me the toolkit, and we'll gladly share it on my social with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks FDNY for answering questions, praises the department, says the committee will continue working with them, notes DOT's absence and the discontinued trade-in program, and dismisses the panel.
chapters.title: Ariola thanks FDNY panel and dismisses them

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, so I want to thank everyone who came.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: FDMY, thank you for taking the lion's share of the questions and answering them to the best of your ability, and also the lion's share of questions that were not meant for you and answering them to the best of your ability.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We do appreciate everything you do every single day, each and every one of your members.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You are the absolute bravest and best, and that is not lost on me, Chair Sanchez, our speaker, or this committee and the other committees and the members of our council.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So we're going to continue to work with you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I appreciate the fact that you're not opposed vehemently to any of the bills and that you're willing to work with us because that's what these hearings are about, so that we work together so that we can have a comprehensive package.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Each of these bills complement the other and add an extra layer of safety.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So, yes, we want to be reasonable.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We want to be able to get it done.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We want to make sure they are both functional and viable.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We're not asking for what's not available to us.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: But we can really, where I think we were at the weakest is the fact that DOT is not here and that program, and thank you for getting the information, FDMY, about the program,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: and the fact that it wasn't continually funded.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And that's something that we can look at as well, because that is a very important program where there can be an exchange for these batteries at no cost to people who are using them.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We want to save lives.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We want to make sure that our first responders'lives are not put in further danger.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And I thank you all for coming here today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Chair, can I just correct an earlier statement I made?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So with regard to the information about lithium ion batteries that we provide tenants, I misspoke and we do in fact provide it in the 10 languages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Oh, wonderful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Hard copy format.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I hope that addresses your concern.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I believe that this panel can be dismissed.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And thank you, Commissioner, for bringing such a comprehensive, well-informed team with you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And yourself being so well-informed.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, we just have a lot of movement for people leaving, so we're going to wait a second and then get to our public testimony.

chapters.summary: Ariola opens public testimony, reminds the public to remain silent unless testifying, explains witness table rules, appearance cards, two-minute speaking limit, and how to submit written testimony.
chapters.title: Ariola opens public testimony and explains rules

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, we're ready for the public testimony portion.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We will now open the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times unless they're testifying.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, if you haven't already, fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today's oversight hearing topic, residential fires and the dangers of lithium-ion batteries and related legislation.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to testimony at council.nyc.gov.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: That's testimony at council.nyc.gov.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Within 72 hours of the close of this hearing,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: For in-person panelists, please come up to the table once your name has been called, and I will now call the first panel.

chapters.summary: Ariola calls the UFA and UFOA panel. Spillane, chief representative for the Uniform Fire Officers Association, says fatal lithium-ion battery fires have reached epidemic proportions, describes difficult extinguishment and rescue conditions, and cites 619 injuries, 44 fatalities, and 1,600 fires over six years. He calls for better data and correction of New York State law 8832.
chapters.title: Jack Spillane describes lithium-ion battery fires as epidemic

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: President of the UFA, Robert Eustace, and we have, I think, we have Jax Blaine from the UFOA.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Uniformed Firefighters Association and the Uniformed Fire Officers Association.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: To explain the acronym.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: My name is Jack Spillane.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: I am a chief representative for the Uniform Fire Officers Association.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: The amount of fatal lithium-ion battery fires in New York City has reached epidemic proportions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: It seems that every day the FDNY is responding to multiple occupied structural fires across the city due in part to lithium-ion batteries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: Upon arrival on scene, our members are met with an advanced fire that is extending from its ignition source to the building's upper floors and possibly to other nearby structures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: When these fires occur in occupied residential buildings, the increasingly difficult extinguishment effort takes place in conjunction with life-saving search and rescue operations being executed in high heat and smoke conditions and an ever-expanding fire scene.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: These fires become more stressful during the overnight hours due to the expected civilian life hazard of sleeping residents, which is exacerbated when occurring in non-fireproof buildings with a single staircase for access and egress.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: Many times, occupancy entrances and exit points are used for e-bike storage, which creates an even greater life hazard as the expected exit is blocked by fire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: According to the FDNY and the New York City Council, over the past six years, there have been 619 people injured and at least 44 fatalities and 1,600 in a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: 11 lithium ion battery fires.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: These are staggering numbers, yet they reflect only a portion of the human toll resulted from these fires.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: Further questions need to be asked to accurately reflect the impact on survivors of these fires.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: The Fire Department and New York City Housing and Buildings need to formalize information sharing to reflect the real effect of lithium-ion battery fires.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: Namely, how many buildings with battery fires are only occupied, rental, or NYCHA?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: Do the fires originate near access and egress points?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: How many units of housing have been lost due to lithium-ion battery fires?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: What is the amount of property loss due to the fire and extinguishing efforts?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: The percentage of damage to the building is at a total loss.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: And how much time does it take for a building to be reoccupied and reconstructed?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: These questions must be asked to get a complete picture of the impact of these fires on survivors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: The only fault was they lived in or adjacent to a building where someone kept and charged an e-bike with a faulty battery.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: The prevalence of substantial lithium-ion batteries has created a public health and property crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: More needs to be done to protect the citizens of New York City and its firefighters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: The UFOA would like to thank Speaker Menon, the committee members, Ariola and Perina Sanchez, and...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: As holding this hearing, we ask the members of this committee to appeal to their state legislative partners to correct New York State 8832, which was signed to law earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: This law allows for the storage of used and possibly defective lithium-ion batteries at the point of purchase.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: Many of these stores are in non-fireproof buildings with apartments above.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: Although passed with good intentions, we believe this law could have the unintended consequences of placing numerous possibly defective batteries in a mostly residential building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: A lithium-ion battery in such a building could lead to catastrophe, as we well know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: The UFOI would like to acknowledge the bipartisan efforts of Congressman Richie Torres, who sponsored H.R.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: 973, Senate Consumer Standards for Lithium-Ion Batteries Act, which passed, which asked the Consumer Product Safety Commission to establish minimum safety standards for manufacturers and distributors of lithium-ion batteries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: This bill passed overwhelmingly in the House with help from Representative Andrew Garbarino.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: Additional thanks to Senators Gillibrand and Schumer for shepherding this legislation through the Senate, where it passed with strong bipartisan support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: Now awaits the President's signature.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: Hopefully their work and the work of the City Council will curb the influx of these deadly low-grade batteries that are plaguing the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Spillane
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks Spillane and calls Bobby Eustace. Eustace, president of the Uniformed Firefighters Association, says the city is not doing enough, reads from FDNY manuals about hose line positioning, and argues adding a fifth firefighter to every engine would save lives in fast-moving lithium-ion battery fires. He asks for a $6 million Bronx pilot and says seconds matter.
chapters.title: Bobby Eustace calls for fifth firefighter on every engine

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: There we go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Thank you for having me today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: My name is Bobby Eustace.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: I'm the president of the Uniform Firefighter Association and a proud first responder and firefighter in the Bronx for the past 25 years, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: You started this conversation, this hearing today by asking, are you doing enough?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Are you doing everything?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: That answer is clearly no.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: These firefighters, the lithium-ion batteries, they start off, they go off like a blowtorch.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: They're faster than anything we've had before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: I want to read something from the FDNY books, Basic Engine Ops, Chapter 1.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Quote, more lives are saved at fire operations by proper positioning and operating the hose lines than all other life-saving techniques available to firefighting forces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Nothing does anything, saves more lives than putting the water on the fire faster.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Nothing does that faster than more firefighters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Simple end stop.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: There isn't a firefighter book in the world or any other department that will tell you anything different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: When the fire department has any emergencies, they add the fifth firefighter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: We started trying to add that to the budget, and we started this process years ago, and we've asked for that funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: We are talking about pennies on the dollar here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Seconds matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Every time you watch a film, you watch these fires rise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: The rest of that first is the first paragraph in the first book we read in Proby School.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Engine company operations are the foundation of all firefighting efforts in the FDNY.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: A full understanding of these operations is essential to the continued success of the department and preservation of life and property in the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: We are sworn to take an oath to protect life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: from property in New York City Fire Department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: That's what we do as New York City firefighters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: That's what we do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: The stretching and operating of hose lines is the primary function of an engine company.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: All members must realize the importance of the initial stretch of the structural fire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: That is what we do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: This is what we need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: We need the fifth firefighter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: In the Bronx, we asked for a pilot program for $6 million.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: It would cost

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: I guess under $80 million.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: We have the many, many programs throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: The Office of Mass Engagement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: We would love to mass engage the extra 40 people that died a year to date.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: 51 people died a year to date this year, last year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: We're at 90 now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: We would love to spend that money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: We're not about taking money from anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: But we are nickel and diming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: I also find it shocking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: And by the way, I want to say, I think the department is doing everything they can with the resources they are provided.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: But isn't it a little shocking they didn't ask for a nickel more?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: I think that's a little shocking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Not a nickel more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: We're not doing enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Clearly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Tonight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: At 6 p.m., you can add the fifth firefighter to every engine in New York City for a couple shekels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Is that worth the life to save for someone in a lithium-ion battery fire?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Because we also know that the black market is out there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Even the first deputy commissioner testified, these are coming more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: These batteries are aging out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: These fires are coming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: So if we know they're coming,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: The fatal fire in the Bronx, someone who's dead on scene, two more dead in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Seconds matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Maybe we could have got to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Maybe we couldn't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: But we won't know if we didn't try.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Are we going to try?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bobby Eustace
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks Eustace and agrees on the need for a fifth firefighter. Sanchez calls Wendy Kinkade. Kinkade says she is the aunt of the first family killed in the Bronx e-bike fire and is preparing to bury four family members. She faults gig-work companies like Amazon, Uber Eats, and DoorDash for not providing safe transportation, says her niece got an e-bike from a friend, and urges immediate legislation and better city support for grieving families.
chapters.title: Wendy Kinkade mourns family killed in Bronx e-bike fire and blames gig companies

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Very compelling, and it is true.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We do need the fifth firefighter.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'd next like to call up Wendy Kinkade.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: I am the aunt of the first family that was tragically killed by this horrific e-bike accident in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: I'm here to bury dead four members of my family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: The first funerals start tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: This is the hardest thing that I have had to do in a long time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: It is imperative that you pass laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: And not only I can understand, I spoke with the commissioner about what's going on,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: but what you have to understand is I fault a lot of this to the gig work that's going on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: These multi-million dollar corporations like Amazon, eBay, I'm not eBay, Uber Eats,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: DoorDash, they have the money to provide the transportation for these folks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: Prior to this event happening to my family, I had a conversation with my niece that passed away, Saida.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: And I told her, she said, Auntie, I need to make some money because things are really tight right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: I had been sending her money every week to keep the family going.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: And one of the things she said to me is she said, well, we could get a job working for Amazon doing deliveries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: I told her, no, don't do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: If you're going to work for Amazon, go to the warehouse and work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: And I think because she was so adamant and they were so adamant that they could make more money doing deliveries that they went and got this e-bike from a friend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: And this caused their lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: I hope that the legislation goes after these third party companies because they're the culprit in this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: They sit back and make millions of dollars on the backs of individuals who are desperate to find a way to feed their families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: And unless you make some kind of legislation against them, I don't fault the people like my niece and my nephew.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: He's still struggling, fighting for his life in Harlem Hospital right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: Four, three children are gone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: I have to look at a coffin tomorrow with my nephew and my niece in it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: I'm going today when I leave here to the funeral home, to Benta's funeral home, to view the bodies to make sure that they're okay for tomorrow's ceremony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: I shouldn't have to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: No one should have to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: The people in Sunset Park should not have to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: Legislation can be passed, and it needs to be passed, whether you have the departments agreeing upon it or not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: It needs to be passed and it needs to be passed right away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: Because no one should go through what we're going through.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: Not only have we lost family members, this is a costly event for our family to try to get the funds together to bury four members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: Imagine what's going on with the people in Sunset Park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: And I reached out to the local leaders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
