utterances.text: I reached out to Vanessa Gibson's office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: I sent you an email.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: I sent the speaker an email.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: Nobody responded to us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: The only person that responded to us was Carl Hastings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: His office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: So you guys need to do better also, especially when you have tragedies at this magnitude.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: Families need someone that they could talk to, a liaison within the city government that they could talk to and not be put on a loop on the phone saying, oh, well, we can't help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: We can't do this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: Sometimes everyone is not going for monetary help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: They're just trying to navigate the things that are going on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: We still haven't been able to get into the apartment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: because it's still locked, to see if there's anything retrievable that was belonging to my family, to see, make sure that their stuff gets out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: I don't know how else to express the importance of your job, because my job begins tonight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: I will return, I'm a native New Yorker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: I left, I was in law enforcement in New York City for 20 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: I retired in 2006 after I served for 9-11.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: And I moved out of the state.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: I live in Georgia now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: I had to come up here to make sure that everything is all right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: I want you guys to enforce this legislation, and I want to hold your feet to the fire to make sure that legislation happens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: Because nobody needs to go through this again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: No, not one family, not one individual need to go through this again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: People have to make a living, and they should be able to make a living safely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: And if these third-party companies want people to follow their business model, then you enforce the laws on them that their business model has to be conducive to the safety of the people of this state and every other state in this country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: Because this is not just happening here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Kinkade
utterances.text: It's happening all over this country.

chapters.summary: Sanchez thanks Kinkade and apologizes for lack of response. Ariola offers condolences and calls the next panel. Chuck Thompson, director of fire safety solutions at eFire USA, describes the eFire Vault Series for charging and storing lithium-ion batteries, and says small companies face barriers getting innovative fire safety solutions reviewed by New York City. He asks for a more accessible and transparent process.
chapters.title: Chuck Thompson asks for fair evaluation of innovative fire safety products

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Wendy.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much for being with us today.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I am so sorry for your loss.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Look into why you haven't gotten a response from us.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But thank you for sharing because your testimony is going to change what we do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We do here today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Yes, deepest condolences.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The next panel is Kelly Barajas, Jerry Kestenbaum, John Orlando, Lucy Corthell, and Chuck Thompson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Left to right, right to left.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: I guess I'm going first.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: I'm just going to read a statement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: My name is Chuck Thompson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: I'm the director of fire safety solutions at eFire USA, a small minority-owned fire safety company based in Brewster, New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: Our mission has been the same since day one, bring innovation to fire safety because you can never have enough fire protection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: Believe our safety should go beyond simple meeting of minimum requirements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: It should embrace innovation, identify risks before they become tragedies, introduce additional layers of protection that help reduce property damage,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: environmental impact, and most importantly, potential loss of life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: Our approach is simple.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: Identify risk, design, and the solution add layers of protection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: We have worked with companies across renewable energy, manufacturing, agricultural, waste management, transportation, and marine industries, and recognize the realities of fire and the importance of innovation in protective solutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: I want to applaud New York City for its efforts to address fire safety, particularly growing dangers associated with lithium batteries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: I am here today to raise concerns about something we believe deserves greater attention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: How do innovative fire safety solutions get a fair opportunity to be evaluated and considered by New York City?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: Years ago, eFire USA introduced the eFire Vault Series, designed to provide additional protection when charging lithium and storing lithium-ion battery-powered equipment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: Vault incorporates steel construction, smoke detection, audible alarms, automatic power shutoff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: It is designed to provide early warning and additional layer protection when battery-related incidents occur.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: We recognize that no single product eliminates the dangers associated with lithium batteries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: That is precisely why we believe a layered fire protection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: Unfortunately, as a small company, gaining access to appropriate decision makers in New York City to demonstrate and evaluate an innovative fire safety solution has been extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: For two years, we have actively pursued opportunities to introduce eFire Vault to the city and to the state.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: With little success, instead, we have repeatedly encountered the very problem we are here to address, a process that creates barriers and delays, limiting opportunities for innovative products to be seen, demonstrated, or properly

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: evaluated on their merits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: We understand the importance of codes, certifications, testing, and regulatory oversight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: Many of these requirements exist for very good reasons, and we support them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: But there is a difference between maintaining rigorous safety standards and creating a process where innovative solutions struggle to receive even initial technical review.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: Too often the process becomes a series of forums, questions, and certification requirements without a clear pathway to evaluation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: Meanwhile, lithium battery fires continue to threaten property and lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: eFire USA believes strongly in independent testing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: In fact, we are investing our own resources in third-party testing of the eFire vault.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: We are not asking the city to overlook the certification requirements, wave safety standards, or approve an untested product.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: We are asking for a pathway that allows innovative products to be reviewed, demonstrated, tested, and evaluated for their merits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: There may be solutions available today or emerging technologies under development that could make meaningful contributions to fire safety tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: Those solutions deserve a process that encourages responsible innovation rather than unintentionally discouraging it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: Our philosophy has never been replacing a single fire safety equipment or establishing protections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: It is to strengthen them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: Compliance should be the foundation of fire safety, not the ceiling.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: We ask the City Council to consider establishing a more accessible and transparent process through which smaller fire safety companies like ours can present emerging technologies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: to the appropriate city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just wanted to make sure everybody's mindful of the clock.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, that's it.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, and you can submit your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chuck Thompson
utterances.text: It's been submitted.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Perfect, perfect.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Kestenbaum says he has developed a lithium battery sensor that can warn 5 to 15 minutes before a battery catches fire. He suggests the city gather universities for a hackathon or standing technology committee to create an inexpensive device that alerts people to battery distress.
chapters.title: Jerry Kestenbaum offers lithium battery sensor and hackathon idea

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: Jerry Kestenbaum, I've written to some of you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: I'm not here to ask for anything.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: I'm here to offer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: I am one of the leading successful people in New York City who's launched three companies building native new technology that pioneered for buildings, building safety, leak detection, building link software.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: We have a leak sensor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: We have a local 157 natural gas sensor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: And we have a lithium battery sensor that will tell you about 5 to 15 minutes before a battery catches fire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: Maybe not suited for a house, but very suited for a garage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: There are some very interesting issues with fires with cars.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: When you have a garage that's half electric, half gasoline, and they're all made of plastic, a lithium battery fire in Seoul, Korea in 2024 set 600 cars on fire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: Interesting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: Anyway, what I was going to suggest is as follows.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: In addition to all the issues of non-compliant batteries, even a compliant battery, when it is subjected to stress, can break down.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: That affects bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: It affects...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: It affects electronic wheelchairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: 45% of wheelchairs now have lithium batteries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: You'll find on YouTube a video of a wheelchair exploding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: And it involves electrical cars in garages with gas cars on top of buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: What I was going to suggest is an alternate approach, maybe similar to what this gentleman was saying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: If the city wishes to gather its universities and create a little hackathon,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: or a standing technology committee, like Minerva Tantico used to do years ago,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: to explore how can you create an inexpensive device that will let you know that a battery is going into distress.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: Whether it's temperature, whether it's deformation,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: whether it's voltage drops, it is absolutely possible to create a $20 device that you could strap onto your battery that will give you a minute or two notice and a siren in the middle of the night.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: A hundred of these 250 lives probably could have been saved if people were woken up and got the hell out of there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Kestenbaum
utterances.text: I'm available to help in any capacity.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you for your offer.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We appreciate that.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks Kestenbaum and calls John Orlando. Orlando, retired FDNY supervising fire marshal and chair of SAE Micromobility Battery Standards Committee, says Intro 582 should require certified containers under UL 1487. He also calls for amending Intro 2030 to create a registration process for e-bike and scooter owners to help enforcement and building access.
chapters.title: John Orlando recommends certified cabinets and e-bike registration

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs, for having me before you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: I'm John Orlando.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: I retired in 2024 from the FDNY with 27 years of service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: I was the supervising fire marshal of the Lithium Ion Task Force and director of training for the Bureau of Fire Investigation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: Upon retirement, I founded Orlando Safety Solutions, and I continue teaching, consulting, and speaking about lithium-ion battery safety, fire service challenges, and solutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: I am currently the chair of the SAE Micromobility Battery Standards Committee and a member of the UL Technical Committee for Vehicle Systems for Electric Scooters and Motorcycles, TC 2850.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: I also recently, October 21st, testified at the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: Consumer Product Safety

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: Commission's hearing on standards and safety in the micromobility battery industry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: Intro 582, part of the legislative package, would require employers to provide fire-resistant charging containers for removable batteries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: However, the legislation does not mandate these containers be certified according to existing standards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: And on the summary, it says fireproof or fire-resistant containers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: Let's just remember why we're here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: Lithium-ion batteries are not like traditional fires.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: They create their own oxygen in a confined space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: They will continue to burn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: They deflagrate, explode.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: They create an explosive environment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: The venting, there needs to be venting, and there needs to be controlling of the flame, which will jet out of a cabinet, which can then extend to surrounding buildings, structures, vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: So we need to just amend that to be certified cabinets, the 1487.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: I'm happy to talk more about that at a later date.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: And the second is I'm also calling for an amendment to Intro 2030, which was to establish outreach inspection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: I believe the legislation must incorporate a registration process for anyone owning an e-bike or scooter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: A lot was discussed about enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: And one of the issues in private dwellings is we can't get into them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: So having an amendment to require registration would tell us where these bikes are, and I'm not looking to make it punitive or punishing, just to say that maybe we just confiscate them from the people, and it gives cover to buildings to be able to say, you can't bring this in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: into the building if it's not registered as a certified device.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: So those are my main comments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: I'm happy to discuss them.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much for sharing your expertise and common sense.

chapters.summary: Sanchez thanks Orlando and says she likes the hackathon idea. Ariola calls the next panel. Fowler, senior advisor to Swabi, says the city cannot expect people to stop charging at home without practical alternatives. He describes Swabi's fire-safe battery swapping hub at City Hall Park, which completed nearly 6,000 swaps in 30 days, and argues battery swapping should be treated as essential infrastructure to scale.
chapters.title: Tom Fowler argues safe battery swapping must scale as essential infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I like the idea of a hackathon.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Maybe we can work on this.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Our next panel consists of Tom Fowler, David Hammer, Corey Hannigan, Jonathan Cohen, and Juan Restrepo.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: My name is Tom Fowler.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: I'm a senior advisor to Swabi, a company that develops and operates fire safe battery swapping infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: I'd like to suggest that New York look at this horrific problem through a new lens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: We talk about dangerous batteries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: We talk about enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: We talk about confiscation, education, and penalties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: Those things have their place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: But here's the fundamental problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: We cannot expect people to stop charging batteries in their homes if we don't give them a practical, affordable, and accessible alternative.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: Thousands of New Yorkers, including the 80,000 delivery workers operating in the city every day,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: depend on e-bikes to earn a living.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: And we depend on them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: These are the people delivering food and products to each of us every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: To do their jobs, their batteries need charging, often multiple times per day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: No amount of e-bike

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: confiscation or battery confiscation is going to change that fact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: So the better question is how can New York City make safe charging the obvious and most practical choice?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: And to that question, I have some very encouraging news.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: The city and SWABI already know how to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: And together, we're already doing it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: Just a few steps from this room, at the Deliverista Hub in City Hall Park, SWAB operates a fire-safe battery swapping infrastructure that delivery workers use every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: In the last 30 days alone, workers completed nearly 6,000 battery swaps at that single location.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: Think about what that means.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: Instead of taking batteries home to charge in bedrooms and kitchens, workers exchange depleted, UL certified, professionally maintained batteries for charged ones in seconds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: And this takes place at outdoor cabinets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: The entire system managed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: and monitored by trained professionals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: The key innovation isn't just the battery, it's the fire safe system around the battery.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: We're a German company.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: We're based in Berlin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: We've been in business since 2017.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: We're all over Europe.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And I ask you to wrap up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: So the discipline around safety as integral to the product and the solution is how we operate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: We believe that's a core tenet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: The problem today is not the technology which exists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: The problem is scale.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: The question I pose to the council, do we have the will to embrace the scale that solves the problem?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: The technology question has been answered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks Fowler and directs the next speaker. Cohen, co-founder of Joko, says the city's decision not to approve more cabinets until 2028 is harmful because batteries will otherwise be charged in apartments. He says Joko uses UL-certified batteries, bikes, and charging equipment together, similar to Citi Bike, and that roadblocks prevent scaling.
chapters.title: Jonathan Cohen says Joko's UL-certified system faces deployment roadblocks

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Who's going next?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We'll start back here.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Right here.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Want to go there?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Chair, and thank you very much for your time here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: My name is Jonathan Cohen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: I'm the co-founder of Joko.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: We run a New York City network of e-bikes that serve thousands of delivery workers every single day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: I have a written testimony that we submitted, but I'm just going a little off course because I want to echo, Madam Chair, your statement that you made earlier about cabinets

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: not being approved until, no further cabinets being approved until 2028.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: We think that's a, you know,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: a horrible outcome because every single battery that's not going to be charged in safe infrastructure is going to be charged in someone's apartment instead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And we all know what that leads to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: There have tragically been far too many deaths as a result of this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And I echo what my colleague was saying, what my friend here was saying earlier from Swabi, that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: that technology does exist and we just haven't been able to scale and there have been far too many roadblocks in the way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: I would just tell you a little bit more about Joko.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: So at Joko we have the only system in the city

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: that utilizes UL certified batteries, UL certified bikes, and UL certified charging equipment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And all three are used together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And it's actually very important that all three are used together because you can't use a non-UL certified battery inside a non-UL certified

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: Sorry, a UL-certified battery and a non-UL-certified bike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: In fact, it's nearly identical to the city's city bike system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: That's the system that we operate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And as we all know, city bike has a stellar safety record, and not a single battery from city bike or Joko is ever brought into anyone's apartment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: It cannot be brought into anyone's apartment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: Unfortunately, as I mentioned before, there are far too many roadblocks to scale.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: The solutions are here, but we really need to challenge the city to scale those.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And we're here to speak with you, and we'd really, really love to speak with you to solve these issues and eliminate these unnecessary deaths.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks Cohen and calls Corey Hannigan. Hannigan of Transportation Alternatives says uncertified batteries are the main cause of fires but banning devices or punishing users will not work. He supports Intro 582, recommends amending Intro 1189 to focus penalties on sellers, opposes Intro 920, and calls for a robust buyback and expanded safe charging and battery swap stations.
chapters.title: Corey Hannigan urges buyback, safe charging, and opposes punitive bills

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: My name is Corey Hannigan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: I'm the Policy and Government Relations Director for Safe Streets at Transportation Alternatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: So we're obviously here today to talk about the terrifying battery fires that are plaguing our city and by all accounts appear to be increasing in number.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: The vast majority of these fires, as we know, start with dangerous, uncertified batteries used to power mopeds and other high-speed devices, as well as some e-bikes and e-scooters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: But we can't talk about these fires without discussing New Yorkers'growing demand for delivered food, the rising popularity of e-bikes and other forms of micromobility, and the proliferation of cheap, uncertified, illegal devices masquerading as safe and legal ones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: There are some 70,000 delivery workers in this city, the vast majority of them low-income, predominantly immigrant workers that rely on e-bikes, e-scooters, mopeds, and other battery-powered devices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: But they aren't the only ones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: As of 2024, at least 38% of New York City households own at least one bike, 20% own two or more, and one in 10 of them owns an e-bike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: The numbers alone show that electric mobility is here to stay and that this problem cannot be solved by banning battery-powered devices or punishing those who rely on them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: Many of the bills being heard today focus on punitive measures, but merely punishing people with dangerous batteries will not rid our city of them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: It'll just cause people to conceal these extremely dangerous flammable batteries in dense apartments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: So instead, like others, we feel that we need to address the dangerous batteries already out there by providing solutions that help people transition to safer products and charging practices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: Transportation Alternatives encourages the Council to fund a robust buyback and trade-in program for people in possession of dangerous batteries

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: and to dramatically expand publicly accessible safe charging and battery swap stations for people who rely on electric devices but may live in buildings with subpar electrical systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: In particular, we support Intro 582 requiring delivery businesses to provide workers with fire-resistant containers for their batteries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: We recommend amending Intro 1189, which penalizes possession, use, and handling of substandard e-bike batteries, just to focus the penalties on those selling the batteries alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: And we oppose Intro 920, which bans storing powered mobility devices in any R2 zone building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: Without wider availability of safe outdoor storage facilities, this would effectively ban safe, legal, low-speed e-bikes in much of eastern Queens, where many residents live far from jobs and out of reach of the subway.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: So just in conclusion, e-bikes and e-scooters are widely possessed and essential mobility devices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: The New Yorkers who are relying on them are counting on the council to provide them with solutions to the dangerous battery problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: So let's not punish people who need our help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: Instead, let's give them safe ways to protect themselves and their neighbors from dangerous fires.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Corey Hannigan
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks Hannigan and calls David Hammer. Hammer, co-founder of Pop Wheels, says batteries need to leave basements and apartments but must have somewhere else to go. Pop Wheels uses fire-safe outdoor cabinets, has done over half a million safe swaps, and cut at-home charging by nearly 90%. He asks the Council for a deployment pathway, one agency point of contact, and quarterly public reporting.
chapters.title: David Hammer describes Pop Wheels outdoor battery swapping and asks for scale

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Let's go.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Who's next?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - John Orlando
utterances.text: Hi there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: Thank you, Chief Areola, Chair Sanchez, members of the council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: I'm David Hammer, the co-founder of Pop Wheels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: We are a Brooklyn-based small business founded to solve the fire crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: It's simple.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: Batteries need to get out of basements, apartments, bodegas, and bike shops.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: But this will only work if you give them somewhere else to go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: And that's what we've built with Pop Wheels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: Riders give up their old battery on the day they use us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: They start by checking out a UL-certified battery from a fire-safe outdoor cabinet and swap it for a new one when it's empty.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: Every battery is constantly monitored, and if one overheats, uniquely our cabinet can actually put it out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: We think it's the safest place for a battery to be in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: And it works.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: Just in the past year, thousands of riders have done more than half a million safe swaps in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: New York City DOT determined that our riders cut at-home charging by nearly 90%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: Moving charging into proven outdoor infrastructure, whether ours or the other operators who are here, will save lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: But to materially impact the fire crisis, the city needs scale.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: Right now, today, we have hundreds of riders who have put down paid deposits who are waiting to stop charging at home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: But neither we nor the other operators here can serve them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: The regulatory complexity of the city, though well-intentioned, has slowed down our deployments to a crawl.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: Now the city has mandated a standstill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: that no product on the market can meet, grinding progress to a complete standstill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: So riders are staying waiting, and their batteries are staying in apartments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: So I'm asking this council to push for three things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: A pathway, so cabinets that FDNY has already signed off on can keep deploying,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: An agency, one point of contact, who can help expedite deployments, and a public quarterly report on deployments, timelines, and approvals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: None of this lowers core safety standards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: Batteries should not be charged in apartments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: But we need to give riders a better place to go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: I invite any member here or their staff

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: to come visit one of our hubs around New York City and see what's possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how the cabinet can put out an overheating battery. Hammer explains that fully submerging a battery in water contains the exothermic reaction as it runs its course, and says Pop Wheels has tested this at nationally recognized labs.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks how Pop Wheels cabinet extinguishes a battery fire

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Just a quick follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: You said the cabinet can actually put out a battery that's overheating.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: Yeah, we've built our own technology here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: So there's a story here sometimes that water doesn't put out a battery fire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: And that is true.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: If you sprinkle a battery with water, we sometimes compare it to a trick candle for a birthday trick candle, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: It'll go down, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: And so it's referred to as an exothermic reaction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: But if you're able to fully submerge a battery, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: It's not technically extinguishing it in the sense that you think of putting out a fire, but the mass of the water that is containing the fire, it will fully contain it as the chemical reaction runs its course.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: We've tested this at nationally recognized testing labs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: and demonstrated consistently that it does in fact achieve the goal we set out for.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification.

chapters.summary: Sanchez thanks the panel and calls Juan Restrepo. Restrepo of Lime says the company operates the city's shared e-scooter program in Eastern Queens and the East Bronx, has had over 9 million trips without a fire-related injury, uses UL-certified batteries charged in steel cabinets, and offers low-income access programs. He says shared fleets provide a safe alternative to unregulated private devices.
chapters.title: Juan Restrepo says Lime's shared scooters offer safe alternative

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I thought we had started on that side.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Hello, okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Areola, Chair Sanchez, Councilmember Wong, and other members of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: My name is Juan Restrepo, and I lead government relations in New York City for Lime, the world's largest electric mobility shared company.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: We are also the largest operator in the city's shared e-scooter program in Eastern Queens and the East Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Over 400 battery-related fires have destroyed homes and taken the lives of our fellow New Yorkers this year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: We share the council's urgency to stop them, and we hope that what we have learned operating battery-powered shared scooters at scale can be a useful resource in that effort.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: At Lime, we care deeply about the safety of our riders and the broader communities we serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: This is why we design our vehicles and batteries in-house with safety in mind.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Now with over 9 million scooter trips since we started operating Queens in the Bronx, we have not experienced a single fire-related injury.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: All of Lime's batteries are approved to be compliant with international battery safety standards, including UL certification.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: They are handled by trained personnel, including being charged in steel charging cabinets in our local warehouses and swapped using fire suppressive bags in barrels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: One of them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Most important ways to prevent more fires is to reduce the number of dangerous unregulated batteries on our streets and in our homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Having a rentable fleet of battery safe scooters provides a viable alternative to private ownership of unregulated ones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Additionally, safe micromobility options must not only be widely available, but also affordable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Lime Access, our program for low-income New Yorkers, provides free daily rides every day of the month with no cost to sign up or use it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Lime Prime, our monthly membership, offers 20-minute rides for less than the cost of a subway swipe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Access to more than one regulated shared option gives New Yorkers a viable and affordable alternative to uncertified devices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: As the mayor and DOT shared in their Vision Zero Reimagined report, the city would like to bring our scooter program to more parts of the city, and we would love to expand our program as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: As the city council continues to focus on fire safety, Lime is happy to serve as a resource, whether for knowledge sharing about safer battery design or as a provider to help power even more rides in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks several panelists what exactly is prohibiting further deployment of charging cabinets. David Hammer explains FDNY moved from a previous standard to UL 1487, which is strict and requires rebuilding supply chains, causing deployments to stall. Jonathan Cohen adds that letters of no objection come with impractical stipulations and approvals need acceleration.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks what code or agency is blocking cabinet deployment

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And thank you because this gives me the opportunity to ask a clarifying question.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So several of you have said that the city is prohibiting the expansion of any more cabinets for charging.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What exactly is it in which agency, what part of the code, if you have that information available, that is prohibiting from further deployment of these devices?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: I'll give a little bit of context.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: I'm sure Johnny or the Swabby folks can do a little bit as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: So, FDNY spoke to this a little bit before, but again, I can speak for myself and I think I can speak for those folks as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: There was a previous review process for battery cabinets that the FDNY had opened using its own standard that was inspired by a UL standard called UL 9540A, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: We all had to go through it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: You had to set a battery on fire inside the charging cabinet and show that it did not spread to any other slots.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: That standard, about a year and a half ago, UL introduced a brand new standard called UL 1487 that FDNY then proceeded to mandate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: UL 1487 is a long-term, a really good standard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: It is extremely strict.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: It is the strictest standard that's ever been rolled out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: And I know, I can speak for myself, I expect most of the companies here are working hard on developing technology that is compliant with that standard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: But that takes years because it requires completely rebuilding your supply chain from the ground up, completely redoing your technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: And unfortunately, what that means is that in the meantime, deployments have been unable to continue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: So that's been one example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: The other one I would just emphasize is this really isn't about, I mean, there have been challenges with FDNY, but I don't want to point the finger here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: It's not specifically about FDNY in particular.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: This is an emerging technology category.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: And that means when you hit a...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: against DOB, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: When you hit up against the kind of regulations that weren't designed for these types of systems, you just get a lot of ambiguity and slowness as every organization is trying to run into, as trying to unpack those issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Hammer
utterances.text: So I don't know if you folks have anything you want to add to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: Yeah, I would like to echo that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: However, I would also like to say it has been several years since we received our first letter of no objection for our battery charging cabinets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And, you know, the FDNY has a lot on their plate, so they clearly need...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: You know, extra resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And we love, we really love the guys at FDI and they have engaged us a lot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: But at the same time, we think this is a very critical issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And as I said before, and I genuinely mean it, these deaths could have been prevented.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: The solutions have been there for several years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: There just needs to be some kind of push from somewhere that helps the FDNY authorize some of these technologies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And as I said, we've had our letter of objections for several years for our cabinets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: We've done fire testing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: JOCO has done at least a dozen nationally recognized fire tests.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And there's no doubt that if a fire were ever to happen in one of our cabinets, you would be a lot safer than...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: were it to happen in someone's apartment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And so, you know, it's getting approvals, you know, having a letter of no objection is one thing, but it comes with 20 stipulations that are just not practical.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And we've had so many companies, buildings, residential buildings that have asked us for our cabinets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And we say, you know, great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And then we give them the letter of no objection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And they see 20-odd stipulations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And they're like, you know, we'll just ban charging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: But the truth is, they don't ban it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: They ban it, but that doesn't work because this is an essential part of people's lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: So they then have to take the back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: They then.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: Secretly take the batteries into their apartments anyway.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: So that doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: So we have to find a way to accelerate approvals.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm going to follow up offline just to get citations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: I echo what the two gentlemen said, and just to put a point on it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: Heretofore, battery swapping stations have proceeded as more of a commercial exercise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: I would suggest that the opportunity they represent for fire safety should be viewed through a different lens of essential infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: And through that adjusted lens, you end up with a completely different paradigm around what the approval process should look like, how expedient it should be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Fowler
utterances.text: And as I think the gentleman have also said, you can achieve the necessary scale much more rapidly if you think about it as essential infrastructure as opposed to a commercial exercise.

chapters.summary: Ariola calls the next panel. Solis, a leader with Deliveristas Unidos, says delivery workers work more than 12 hours a day and batteries are essential. He says the biggest problem is not having enough safe places to charge, forcing workers to bring batteries home and risk their families and neighbors. He calls for companies to provide safe conditions.
chapters.title: Antonio Solis testifies in Spanish on delivery workers' charging needs

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The next panel is Antonio Martinez, Yadira Sanchez,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Solis
utterances.text: Los trabajadores de entrega trabajamos más de 12 horas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Solis
utterances.text: Al día utilizando nuestras bicicletas eléctricas para mantener a nuestras familias.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Solis
utterances.text: Nuestras baterías son una herramienta esencial para poder trabajar y generar nuestros ingresos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Solis
utterances.text: Uno de los mayores problemas que enfrentamos es no tener suficientes lugares seguros para cargar nuestras baterías.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Solis
utterances.text: Muchas de las veces nos obligan a llevarlas a nuestros hogares para recargarlas, poniendo en riesgo nuestra seguridad, la de nuestras familias y la de nuestros vecinos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Solis
utterances.text: Como trabajadores queremos cumplir con las normas de seguridad, pero también necesitamos que las empresas asuman su responsabilidad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Solis
utterances.text: y nos proporcionen las condiciones necesarias para trabajar de manera segura.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Solis
utterances.text: No es justo que después de trabajar jornadas tan largas tengamos que preocuparnos por cómo cargar nuestras baterías de manera segura o arriesgar la seguridad de nuestras familias.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Solis
utterances.text: Por eso,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Solis
utterances.text: Necesitamos soluciones para proteger tanto a los trabajadores como a nuestras comunidades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Solis
utterances.text: La seguridad no debe ser responsabilidad exclusiva de los trabajadores.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Solis
utterances.text: Las empresas también deben asumir su parte.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Solis
utterances.text: Muchas gracias por escuchar nuestras voces y apoyar a los trabajadores de entrega de Nueva York.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Batteries are essential for us to be able to work and maintain our incomes.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: One of our biggest problems is not having a place to charge our batteries, putting ourselves at risk, as well as our neighbors.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We want to do our part, but corporations should also support us in working safely.

chapters.summary: Staff thanks Solis and calls the next person. Yadira Sanchez of the Workers' Justice Project says delivery workers care about fire safety but have nowhere else to charge. She says the Deliverista hub outside City Hall safely charges hundreds of batteries daily and warns that Intros 920 and 1189 would punish workers before safe alternatives exist. She urges investment in education, trade-in, and infrastructure.
chapters.title: Yadira Sanchez says workers need safe outdoor charging, not penalties

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Next person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: Good afternoon, members of the City Council Committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: My name is Yadira Sanchez, and I am here today representing the Workers'Justice Project and the more than 70,000 delivery workers who keep New York City running.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: Every day, I speak with workers who spend many hours on their e-bikes in all kinds of weather.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: I can tell you firsthand, nobody cares more about fire safety than the workers themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: Their e-bikes are their livelihoods, and their apartments are where their families sleep.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: They do not want unsafe batteries in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: They just have nowhere else where to charge them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: While we support the City Council goal of preventing fires, legislation alone will not keep people safe if workers have no safe alternatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: The real solution is expanding safe outdoor battery charging and secure parking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: There is a Deliverista hub vital side of City Hall.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: And for this hub, the workers and WJP fought through months to install safely charged, install outdoor charging cabinets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: Today, those cabinets safely charge hundreds of batteries every single day, and workers use them because they want

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: to be safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: This is why bills like Intro 1920 and 1189 are so concerning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: Banning indoor charging in residential buildings and finding workers before safe outdoor options exist puts families in an impossible position, risk a fine or lose their ability to earn a living.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: In a state of punishing workers, the city

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: We should invest in education, battery trading programs, and create more infrastructure to keep batteries in good condition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: Please come and visit our hub right outside this building to see how well safe outdoor charging works.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: Let's build infrastructure workers need to keep themselves, their families, and our city safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yadira Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Herms, deputy director of Workers' Justice Project, supports the bills' goal but says they will not succeed without safe outdoor charging. She says FDNY regulations make it nearly impossible to install cabinets, citing the lengthy approval process for the delivery hub, which now charges over 200 batteries a day with no fires. She opposes Intros 920 and 1189.
chapters.title: April Herms says FDNY regulations block outdoor charging cabinets

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: I can go next.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: I'm April Herms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: I'm the Deputy Director at Workers'Justice Project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: You already know we represent delivery workers, and you already know that safe lithium-ion battery charging is a top priority for workers who spend so much time on e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: We strongly support the goal of all of the bills before the Council today of reducing these indoor fires, and we're eager to work with the Council and FDNY and the administration to make that goal a reality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: However, by themselves, this legislation will not succeed in preventing lithium-ion battery fires.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: The best way to do that, as many people have said, is to get charging out of apartment buildings and provide safe outdoor charging options for workers and everyone else who uses these batteries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: The current FDNY regulations, though, make it nearly impossible for building owners, businesses, and others to install outdoor charging cabinets, as we experienced during the lengthy process of obtaining approval for the charging cabinets in our delivery hub.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: In only two minutes, I can't walk you through that whole process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: But if you have any questions, I'm happy to answer questions about those barriers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: The cabinets now charge over 200 batteries a day, almost 6,000 batteries in a month with no fires.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: We cannot emphasize enough how much we want to champion this outdoor model for charging for delivery workers and everyone else.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: We don't want anyone charging at home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: We also have serious concerns about interest 920 and 1189 for many of the reasons that people have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: If you ban indoor charging in our two buildings without providing meaningful alternatives, people don't have anywhere to go to charge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: And targeting owners of these devices with civil penalties when they may not even know they have an unsafe battery

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: will be far less effective in eliminating the devices than a program focusing on education and a trade-in program that lets them get rid of these devices so they can come forward with them and not hide them and charge them in their apartments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: So eliminating safe e-bike battery fires is a top priority for us and for delivery workers, and we strongly urge the council and the administration to streamline regulations that will fast-track the expansion of safe outdoor charging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: And as Yadira said, we invite you to join us after this outside of our delivery hub to see that in action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Sanchez arranges translation for the next testimony. Jalloh, a delivery worker, says the work is hard with traffic, weather, and pressure, and workers lack basic safety infrastructure. He opposes Intros 920 and 1189 unless workers have safe charging, and calls for expanded DOT- and FDNY-approved public charging hubs and battery swapping cabinets.
chapters.title: Cerno Jalloh describes delivery work risks and calls for charging hubs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cerno Jalloh
utterances.text: We spend long hours waiting in traffic, dealing with bad weather, dangerous streets and the pressure to complete order.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cerno Jalloh
utterances.text: We do this work every day in spite of not having the basic infrastructure we need to stay safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cerno Jalloh
utterances.text: They have provided us with nothing and put us at risk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cerno Jalloh
utterances.text: We have no job security and risk being deactivated for any reason.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cerno Jalloh
utterances.text: We cannot pass bail like into 920 and 1189, banning apartment charging if work have nowhere safe to charge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cerno Jalloh
utterances.text: The city must expand DOT and FDNY approved public charging hub and battery swiping cabinet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cerno Jalloh
utterances.text: This is one of the most important

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cerno Jalloh
utterances.text: way to prep the resident battery fire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cerno Jalloh
utterances.text: We also need more protected bike line and place where workers can safely rest and recharge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cerno Jalloh
utterances.text: Charging hub will give us a safe place to take a break, charging us battery up inside to warm up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cerno Jalloh
utterances.text: We are asking the city to recognize our need and invest into the infrastructure that keep us safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cerno Jalloh
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez thanks Jalloh and notes the next testimony will be in French. Anoueh, a DoorDash delivery worker, says workers rely on e-bikes daily but charging is a major problem. Many carry extra batteries and bring them into apartments because there are too few public charging options, endangering families and neighbors. He opposes Intros 920 and 1189 without safe alternatives and calls for expanded public charging and battery swap cabinets.

chapters.summary: El-Duski, a delivery worker with over three years at Uber Eats, says workers cannot be banned from apartment charging without safe alternatives. He is forced to charge at home between shifts because there is nowhere else, and calls for DOT/FDNY-approved public charging hubs and battery swapping cabinets.
chapters.title: Ibrahim El-Duski says workers need safe places to charge and rest

utterances.text: Hey everyone, my name is Ibrahim Tzuki.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ibrahim El-Duski
utterances.text: I'm a delivery with over three years of experience with Uber Eats.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ibrahim El-Duski
utterances.text: And I see you cannot pass bills like 920 and 1189, panic apartment charging if working, and you have no somewhere safe to charge your batteries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ibrahim El-Duski
utterances.text: Expanding DOT FDNY approved public charging hubs and battery swapping cabinets is the way to eliminate residential fire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ibrahim El-Duski
utterances.text: I'm forced to charge my batteries for my e-bike at home between shifts, but

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ibrahim El-Duski
utterances.text: Because that's the only way, the only option for me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ibrahim El-Duski
utterances.text: The streets are our office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ibrahim El-Duski
utterances.text: The apps provide nothing for us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ibrahim El-Duski
utterances.text: We work 10 to 12 hours a day with no space to rest between our orders and recharge our batteries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ibrahim El-Duski
utterances.text: We need the city to create spaces so we can do our job safely with dignity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ibrahim El-Duski
utterances.text: In long days, in the road, we need to carry multiple batteries, returning them at home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ibrahim El-Duski
utterances.text: Winter is approaching.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ibrahim El-Duski
utterances.text: We are given us places to gather with our buildings around our needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ibrahim El-Duski
utterances.text: This makes us safer, our home safer, and our city safer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ibrahim El-Duski
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sow, a delivery worker, says workers face long hours, dangerous traffic, and little job security. They must provide their own equipment and often charge batteries in apartments because there are no safe alternatives. He opposes Intros 920 and 1189 without safe charging and calls for public charging hubs and battery swap cabinets.
chapters.title: Thierno Souleymane Sow testifies in French on delivery worker risks

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thierno Souleymane Sow
utterances.text: Bonjour les membres du City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thierno Souleymane Sow
utterances.text: Je m'appelle Tierno Suleiman So et je suis livreur.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thierno Souleymane Sow

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thierno Souleymane Sow

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thierno Souleymane Sow
utterances.text: Nous avons également très peu de sécurité de l'emploi, nos revenus dépendent des applications et nous pouvons perdre l'accès au travail sans aucun avertissement ni procédure d'appel équitable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thierno Souleymane Sow

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thierno Souleymane Sow

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thierno Souleymane Sow
